div.head: TO HER ROYAL HIGHNESS THE DUCHESS
div.p: MADAM, Poets, however they may be modest otherwise, have always too good an opinion of what they write. The world, when it sees this play dedicated to your Royal Highness, will conclude I have more than my share of that vanity. But I hope the honour I have of belonging to you will excuse my presumption. 'Tis the first thing I have produced in your service, and my duty obliges me to what my choice durst not else have aspired. I am very sensible, madam, how much it is beholding to your indulgence for the success it had in the acting, and your pro- tection will be no less fortunate to it in the printing; for all are so ambitious of making their court to you, that none can be severe to what you are pleased to favour. This universal submission and respect is due to the greatness of your rank and birth; but you have other illustrious qualities which are much more engaging. Those would but dazzle, did not these really charm the eyes and understandings of all who have the happiness to approach you. Authors, on these occasions, are never wanting to publish a particular of their patron's virtues and perfections; but your Royal Highness's are so eminently known, that, did I follow their examples, I should but paint those wonders here of which every one already has the idea in his mind. Besides, I do not think it proper to aim at that in prose which is so glorious a subject for verse; in which hereafter if I show more zeal than skill, it will not grieve me much, since I less passionately desire to be esteemed a poet than to be thought, Madam, Your Royal Highness's most humble, most obedient, and most faithful servant, GEORGE ETHEREGE.

div.head: PROLOGUE
div.p: BY SIR CAR SCROOPE, BARONET Like dancers on the ropes poor poets fare, Most perish young, the rest in danger are; This, one would think, should make our authors wary, But, gamester like, the giddy fools miscarry. A lucky hand or two so tempts 'em on, They cannot leave off play till they're undone. With modest fears a muse does first begin, Like a young wench newly enticed to sin; But tickled once with praise, by her good will, The wanton fool would never more lie still. 'Tis an old mistress you'll meet here to-night, Whose charms you once have look'd on with delight; But now of late such dirty drabs have known ye, A muse o' th' better sort's ashamed to own ye. Nature well drawn, and wit, must now give place To gaudy nonsense and to dull grimace: Nor is it strange that you should like so much That kind of wit, for most of yours is such. But I'm afraid that while to France we go, To bring you home fine dresses, dance, and show, The stage, like you, will but more foppish grow. Of foreign wares why should we fetch the scum When we can be so richly served at home? For, Heav'n be thank'd, 'tis not so wise an age But your own follies may supply the stage. Though often plough'd, there's no great fear the soil Should barren grow by the too frequent toil, While at your doors are to be daily found Such loads of dunghill to manure the ground. 'Tis by your follies that we players thrive, As the physicians by diseases live; And as each year some new distemper reigns, Whose friendly poison helps t'increase their gains So among you there starts up every day Some new unheard-of fool for us to play. Then for your own sakes be not too severe, Nor what you all admire at home, damn here: Since each is fond of his own ugly face, Why should you, when we hold it, break the glass?

div2.head: SCENE I. –
div2.stage: A Dressing-room. A table covered with a toilet; clothes laid ready.
Enter DORIMANT in his gown and slippers, with a note in his hand made up, repeating verses.

sp.speaker: Dorimant

lg.l: Now for some ages had the pride of Spain
Made the sun shine on half the world in vain.

sp.p: What a dull insipid thing is a billet-doux written in cold blood, after the heat of the business is over! It is a tax upon good-nature which I have here been labouring to pay, and have done it, but with as much regret as ever fanatic paid the Royal Aid or Church Duties, 'Twill have the same fate, I know, that all my notes to her have had of late, 'twill not be thought kind enough. Faith, women are i' the right when they jealousy examine our letters, for in them we always first discover our decay of passion. –Hey! Who waits?

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: Sir –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Call a footman.

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: None of 'em are come yet.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Dogs! Will they ever lie snoring a-bed till noon?

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: 'Tis all one, sir: if they 're up, you indulge 'em so they're ever poaching after whores all the morning.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Take notice henceforward, who's wanting in his duty, the next clap he gets, he shall rot for an example. What vermin are those chattering without?

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: Foggy Nan the orange-woman and swearing Tom the shoemaker.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Go; call in that overgrown jade with the flasket of guts before her; fruit is refreshing in a morning.

lg.l: It is not that I love you less
Than when before your feet I lay.

sp.p: How now, Double Tripe! what news do you bring?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: News! Here's the best fruit has come to town t'year; gad, I was up before four a'clock this morning, and bought all the choice i' the market.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The nasty refuse of your shop.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: You need not make mouths at it; I assure you 'tis all culled ware.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The citizens buy better on a holiday in their walk to Totnam.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Good or bad, tis all one; I never knew you commend anything. Lord! would the ladies had heard you talk of 'em as I have done. Here, bid you man give me an angel.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Give the bawd her fruit again.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Well, on my conscience, there never was the like of you. God's my life, I had almost forgot to tell you there is a young gentlewoman lately come to town with her mother, that is so taken with you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Is she handsome?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Nay, gad, there are few finer women, I tell you but so, and a hugeous fortune, they say. Here, eat this peach, it comes from the stone; 'tis better than any Newington y' have tasted.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: This fine woman, I'll lay my life, [Taking the peach.] is some awkward, ill-fashioned, country toad, who, not having above four dozen of black hairs on her head, has adorned her baldness with a large white fruz, that she may look sparkishly in the forefront of the King's box at an old play.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Gad, you'd change your note quickly if you did but see her.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: How came she to know me?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: She saw you yesterday at the Change; she told me you came and fooled with the woman at the next shop.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I remember there was a mask observed me indeed. Fooled, did she say?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Ay, I vow she told me twenty things you said too; and acted with her head and with her body so like you –

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Dorimant, my life, my joy, my darling sin, how dost tou?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Lord! what a filthy trick these men have got of kissing one another!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Why do you suffer this cartload of scandal to come near you and make your neighbours think you so improvident to need a bawd?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Good, now we shall have it! you did but want him to help you; come, pay me for my fruit.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Make us thankful for it, huswife; bawds are as much out of fashion as gentlemen-ushers: none but old formal ladies use the one, and none but foppish old stagers employ the other – go, you are an insignificant brandy bottle.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Nay, there are wrong her, three quarts of canary is her business.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: What you please, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: To him! give him as good as he brings.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Hang him, there is not such another heathen in the town again, except it be the shoemaker without.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I shall see you hold up your hand at the bar next sessions for murder, huswife; that shoemaker can take his oath you are in fee with the doctor's to sell green fruit to the gentry, that the crudities may breed diseases.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Pray give me my money.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Not a penny; when you bring the gentlewoman hither you spoke of, you shall be paid.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: The gentlewoman! the gentlewoman may be as honest as your sisters, for aught as I know. Pray pay me, Mr. Dorimant, and do not abuse me so; I have an honester way of living, you know it.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Was there ever such a resty bawd?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Some jade's tricks she has, but she makes amends when she's in good-humour. Come, tell me the lady's name, and Handy shall pay you.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: I must not, she forbid me.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That's a sure sign she would have you.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Where does she live?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: They lodge at my house.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Nay, then she's in a hopeful way.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Good Mr. Medley, say your pleasure of me, but take heed how you affront my house. God's my life, in a hopeful way!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Prithee, peace! what kind of woman's the mother?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: A goodly grave gentlewoman. Lord! how she talks against the wild young men o' the town! As for your part, she thinks you an arrant devil; should she see you, on my conscience she would look if you had not a cloven foot.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Does she know me?

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Only by hearsay; a thousand horrid stories have been told her of you, and she believes 'em all.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: By the character, this should be the famous Lady Woodvil and her daughter Harriet.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: The devil's in him for guessing, I think.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Do you know 'em?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Both very well; the mother's a great admirer of the forms and civility of the last age.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: An antiquated beauty may be allowed to be out of humour at the freedoms of the present. This is a good account of the mother; pray, what is the daughter?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Why, first she's an heiress, vastly rich.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: And handsome?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: What alteration a twelvemonth may have bred in her I know not, but a year ago she was the beautifullest creature I ever saw; a fine, easy, clean shape; light brown hair in abundance; her features regular; her complexion clear and lively; large wanton eyes; but above all, a mouth that has made me kiss it a thousand times in imagination, teeth white and even, and pretty pouting lips, with a little moisture ever hanging on them, that look like the Provence rose fresh on the bush, ere the morning sun has quite drawn up the dew.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Rapture, mere rapture!

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Nay, gad, he tells you true; she's a delicate creature.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Has she wit?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: More than is usual in her sex, and as much malice. Then she's as wild as you would wish her, and has a demureness in her looks that makes it so surprising.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Flesh and blood cannot hear this, and not long to know her.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I wonder what makes her mother bring her up to town; an old doting keeper cannot be more jealous of his mistress.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: She made me laugh yesterday; there was a judge came to visit 'em, and the old man, she told me, did so stare upon her, and when he saluted her smacked so heartily; who would think it of 'em?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: God a mercy, a judge!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Do 'em right, the gentlemen of the long robe have not been wanting by their good examples to countenance the crying sin o' the nation.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Come, on with your trappings; 'tis later than you imagine.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Call in the shoemaker, Handy.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Good Mr. Dorimant, pay me; gad, I had rather give you my fruit than stay to be abused by that foul-mouthed rogue; what you gentlemen say, it matters not much, but such a dirty fellow does one more disgrace.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Give her ten shillings, and be sure you tell the young gentlewoman I must be acquainted with her.

sp.speaker: Orange-Woman
sp.p: Now do you long to be tempting this pretty creature. Well, heavens mend you!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Farewell, Boga. [Exeunt ORANGE-WOMAN and HANDY.] Dorimant, when did you see your pis-aller , as you call her Mrs. Loveit?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Not these two days.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: And how stand affairs between you?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: There has been great patching of late, much ado; we make a shift to hang together.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I wonder how her mighty spirit bears it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I'll enough, on all conscience; I never knew so violent a creature.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: She's the most passionate in her love, and the most extravagant in her jealousy, of any woman I ever heard of. What note is that?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: An excuse I am going to send her for the neglect I am guilty of.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Prithee read it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: No; but if you will take the pains you may.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: [reads] "I never was a lover of business, but now I have a just reason to hate it, since it has kept me these two days from seeing you. I intend to wait upon you in the afternoon, and in the pleasure of your conversation forget all I have suffered during this tedious absence." This business of yours, Dorimant, has been with a vizard at the playhouse; I have had an eye on you. If some malicious body should betray you, this kind note would hardly make your peace with her.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I desire no better.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Why, would her knowledge of it oblige you?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Most infinitely; next to the coming to a good understanding with a new mistress, I love a quarrel with and old one; but the devil's in't, there has been such a calm in my affairs of late, I have not had the pleasure of making a woman so much as break her fan, to be sullen, or forswear herself these three days.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A very great misfortune. Let me see, I love mischief well enough to forward this business myself; I'll about it presently and though I know the truth of what you've done will set her a-raving, I'll heighten it a little with invention, leave her in a fit o' the mother, and be here again before you're ready.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Pray stay; you may spare yourself the labour; the business is undertaken already by one who will manage it with as much address, and I think with a little more malice than you can.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Who i' the devil's name can this be?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Why the vizard –that very vizard you saw me with.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Does she love mischief so well as to betray herself to spite another?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Not so neither, Medley. I will make you comprehend the mystery: this mask, for a farther confirmation of what I have been these two days swearing to her, made me yesterday at the playhouse make her a promise before her face utterly to break off with Loveit; and because she tenders my reputation, and would not have me do a barbarous thing, has contrived a way to give me a handsome occasion.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She intends, about an hour before me, this afternoon to make Loveit a visit, and (having the privilege, by reason of a professed friendship between 'em) to talk of her concerns.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Is she a friend?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Oh, an intimate friend!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Better and better; pray proceed.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She means insensibly to insinuate a discourse of me, and artificially raise her jealousy to such a height, that transported with the first motions of her passion, she shall fly upon me with all the fury imaginable as soon as ever I enter; the quarrel being thus happily begun, I am to play my art, confess and justify all my roguery, swear her impertinence and ill-humour makes her intolerable, tax her with the next fop that comes into my head, and in a huff march away; slight her, and leave her to be taken by whosoever thinks it worth his time to lie down before her.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: This vizard is a spark, and has a genius that makes her worthy of yourself, Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You rogue there, who sneak like a dog that has flung down a dish, if you do not mend your waiting I'll uncase you, and turn you loose to the wheel of fortune. Handy, seal this, and let him run with it presently.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Since you're resolved on a quarrel, why do you send her this kind note?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: To keep her at home in order to the business. [To the Shoemaker.] How now, you drunken sot?

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: 'Zbud, you have no reason to talk; I have not had a bottle of sack of yours in my belly this fortnight.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: The orange-woman says your neighbours take notice what a heathen you are, and design to inform the bishop and have you burned for an atheist.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: Damn her, dunghill! if her husband does not remove her, she stinks so the parish intend to indict him for a nuisance.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I advise you like a friend, reform your life; you have brought the envy of the world upon you by living above yourself. Whoring and swearing are vices too genteel for a shoemaker.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: 'Zbud, I think you men of quality will grow as unreasonable as the women; you would engross the sins o' the nation; poor folks can no sooner be wicked, but they're railed at by their betters.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Sirrah, I'll have you stand i' the pillory for this libel.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: Some of you deserve it, I'm sure; there are so many of 'em, that our journeymen nowadays, instead of harmless ballads, sin nothing but your damned lampoons.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Our lampoons, you rogue?

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: Nay, good master, why should not you write your own commentaries as well as Cæsar?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: The rascal's read, I perceive.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: You know the old proverb –ale and history.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Draw on my shoes, sirrah.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: Here's a shoe.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Sits with more wrinkles than there are in an angry bully's forehead.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: 'Zbud, as smooth as your mistress's skin does upon her; so strike your foot in home. 'Zbud, if e'er a monsieur of 'em all make more fashionable wear, I'll be content to have my ears whipped off with my own paring-knife.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: And served up in a ragout instead of coxcombs to a company of French shoemakers for a collation.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: Hold, hold! damn 'em, caterpillars! let 'em feed upon cabbage. Come, master, your health this morning next my heart now.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Go, get you home, and govern your family better; do not let your wife follow you to the alehouse, beat your whore, and lead you home in triumph.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: 'Zbud, there's never a man i' the town lives more like a gentleman with his wife than I do. I never mind her motions, she never inquires into mine; we speak to one another civilly, hate one another heartily, and because 'tis vulgar to lie and soak together, we have each of us our several settle-bed.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Give him half-a-crown.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Not without he will promise to be bloody drunk.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: Tope's the word i' the eye of the world, for my master's honour, Robin.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Do not debauch my servants, sirrah.

sp.speaker: Shoemaker
sp.p: I only tip him the wink; he knows an alehouse from a hovel.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: My clothes, quickly.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Where shall we dine to-day?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Where you will; here comes a good third man.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: Your servant, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Gentle sir, how will you answer this visit to your honourable mistress? 'Tis not her interest you should keep company with men of sense, who will be talking reason.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: I do not fear her pardon, do you but grant me yours for my neglect of late.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Though you've made us miserable by the want of your good company, to show you I am free from all resentment, may the beautiful cause of our misfortune give you all the joys happy lovers have shared ever since the world began.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: You wish me in Heaven, but you believe me on my journey to Hell.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You have a good strong faith, and that may contribute much towards your salvation. I confess I am but of an untoward constitution, apt to have doubts and scruples, and in love they are no less distracting than in religion; were I so near marriage, I should cry out by fits as I ride in my coach, Cuckold, Cuckold , with no less fury than the mad fanatic does Glory in Bethlem.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: Because religion makes some run mad, must I live an atheist?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Is it not great indiscretion for a man of credit, who may have money enough on his word, to go and deal with Jews who for little sums make men enter into bonds and give judgments?

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: Preach no more on this text, I am determined, and there is no hope of my conversion.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [to HANDY, who is fiddling about him]. Leave, your unnecessary fiddling; a wasp that's buzzing about a man's nose at dinner is not more troublesome than thou art.

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: You love to have your clothes hang just, sir.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I love to be well dressed, sir; and think it no scandal to my understanding.

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: Will you use the essence, or orange-flower water?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I will smell as I do to-day, no offence to the ladies' noses.

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: Your pleasure, sir.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That a man's excellency should lie in neatly tying of a ribbon or a cravat! How careful's nature in furnishing the world with necessary coxcombs?

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: That's a mighty pretty suit of yours, Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am glad't has your approbation.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: No man in town has a better fancy in his clothes than you have.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You will make me have an opinion of my genius.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: There is a great critic, I hear, in these matters lately arrived piping hot from Paris.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: Sir Fopling Flutter, you mean.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: The same.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: He thinks himself the pattern of modern gallantry.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: He is indeed the pattern of modern foppery.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: He was yesterday at the play, with a pair of gloves up to his elbows and a periwig more exactly curled than a lady's head newly dressed for a ball.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: What a pretty lisp he has!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Ho! that he affects in imitation of the people of quality of France.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: His head stands for the most part on one side, and his looks are more languishing than a lady's when she lolls at stretch in her coach or leans her head carelessly against the side of a box i' the playhouse.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: He is a person indeed of great acquired follies.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: He is like many others, beholding to his education for making him so eminent a coxcomb; many a fool had been lost to the world had their indulgent parents wisely bestowed neither learning nor good breeding on 'em.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: He has been, as the sparkish word is, brisk upon the ladies already; he was yesterday at my Aunt Townley's, and gave Mrs. Loveit a catalogue of his good qualities under the character of a complete gentleman, who, according to Sir Fopling, ought to dress well, dance well, fence well, have a genius for love-letters, an agreeable voice for a chamber, be very amorous, something discreet, but not over-constant.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Pretty ingredients to make an accomplished person.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am glad he pitched upon Loveit.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I wanted a fop to lay to her charge, and this is as pat as may be.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: I am confident she loves no man but you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The good fortune were enough to make me vain, but that I am in my nature modest.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: Hark you, Dorimant; with your leave, Mr. Medley, 'tis only a secret concerning a fair lady.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Your good breeding, sir, gives you too much trouble; you might have whispered without all this ceremony.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: [to DORIMANT]. How stand your affairs with Belinda of late?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She's a little jilting baggage.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: Nay, I believe her false enough, but she's ne'er the worse for your purpose; she was with you yesterday in a disguise at the play.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: There we fell out, and resolved never to speak to one another more.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: The occasion?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Want of courage to meet me at the place appointed. These young women apprehend loving as much as the young men do fighting at first; but once entered, like them too, they all turn bullies straight.

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: [to BELLAIR]. Sir, your man without desires to speak with you.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: Gentlemen, I'll return immediately.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A very pretty fellow this.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: He's handsome, well-bred, and by much the most tolerable of all the young men that do not abound in wit.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Ever well-dressed, always complaisant, and seldom impertinent; you and he are grown very intimate, I see.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: It is our mutual interest to be so: it makes the women think the better of his understanding and judge more favourably of my reputation; it makes him pass upon some for a man of very good sense and I upon others for a very civil person.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: What was that whisper?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: A thing which he would fain have known, but I did not think it fit to tell him; it might have frighted him from his honourable intentions of marrying.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Emilia, give her her due, has the best reputation of any young woman about the town who has beauty enough to provoke detraction; her carriage is unaffected, her discourse modest, not at all censorious nor pretending, like the counterfeits of the age.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She's a discreet maid, and I believe nothing can corrupt her but a husband.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A husband?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Yes, a husband; I have known many women make a difficulty of losing a maidenhead who have afterwards made none of making a cuckold.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: This prudent consideration, I am apt to think, has made you confirm poor Bellair in the desperate resolution he has taken.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Indeed, the little hope I found there was of her, in the state she was in, has made him by my advice contribute something towards the changing of her condition. Enter BELLAIR. Dear Bellair, by heavens I thought we had lost thee; men in love are never to be reckoned on when we would form a company

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: Dorimant I am undone; my man has brought the most surprising news i' the world.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Some strange misfortune is befallen your love.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: My father came to town last night, and lodges i' the very house where Emilia lies.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Does he know it is with her you are in love?

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: He knows I love, but knows not whom, without some officious sot has betrayed me.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Your Aunt Townley is your confidante and favours the business.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: I do not apprehend any ill office from her; I have received a letter, in which I am commanded by my father to meet him at my aunt's this afternoon; he tells me farther he has made a match for me, and bids me resolve to be obedient to his will or expect to be disinherited.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Now's your time, Bellair; never had lover such an opportunity of giving a generous proof of his passion.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: As how, I pray?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Why, hang an estate, marry Emilia out of hand, and provoke your father to do what he threatens; 'tis but despising a coach, humbling yourself to a pair of goloshes, being out of countenance when you meet your friends, pointed at and pitied wherever you go by all the amorous fops that know you, and your fame will be immortal.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: I could find in my heart to resolve not to marry at all.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Fie, fie! that would spoil a good jest and disappoint the well-natured town of an occasion of laughing at you.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: The storm I have so long expected hangs o'er my head and begins to pour down upon me; I am on the rack, and can have no rest till I'm satisfied in what I fear; where do you dine?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: At Long's or Locket's.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: At Long's let it be.

sp.speaker: Bellair
sp.p: I'll run and see Emilia, and inform myself how matters stand; if my misfortunes are not so great as to make me unfit for company, I'll be with you.

div2.stage: Enter a Footman with a letter.

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: [to DORIMANT]. Here's a letter, sir.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The superscription's right: For Mr. Dorimant .

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Let's see: the very scrawl and spelling of a true-bred whore.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I know the hand; the style is admirable, I assure you.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Prithee read it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [reads]. "I told a you you dud not love me, if you dud, you would have seen me again e'er now; I have no money, and am very mallicolly; pray send me a guynie to see the operies. Your servant to command, Molly."

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Pray let the whore have a favourable answer, that she may spark it in a box and do honour to her profession.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She shall, and perk up i' the face of quality. Is the coach at door?

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: You did not bid me send for it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Eternal blockhead! [HANDY offers to go out.] Hey, sot.

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: Did you call me, sir?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I hope you have not just exception to the name, sir?

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: I have sense, sir.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Not so much as a fly in winter. –How did you come, Medley?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: In a chair.

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: You may have a hackney coach if you please, sir.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I may ride the elephant if I please, sir; call another chair, and let my coach follow to Long's.

div2.stage: [Exeunt singing, Be calm, ye great parents, etc.

div2.head: SCENE I
div2.stage: Enter my Lady TOWNLEY and EMILIA.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: I was afraid, Emilia, all had been discovered.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: I tremble with the apprehension still.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: That my brother should take lodgings i' the very house where you lie!

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: 'Twas lucky we had timely notice to warn the people to be secret; he seems to be a mighty good-humoured old man.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: He ever had a notable smirking way with him.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: He calls me rogue, tells me he can't abide me, and does so bepat me.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: On my word you are much in his favour then.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: He has been very inquisitive, I am told, about my family, my reputation, and my fortune.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: I am confident he does not i' the least suspect you are the woman his son's in love with.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: What should make him then inform himself so particularly of me?

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: He was always of a very loving temper himself; it may be he has a doting fit upon him; who knows?

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: It cannot be.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Here comes my nephew. Where did you leave your father?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Writing a note within. Emilia, this early visit looks as if some kind jealousy would not let you rest at home.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: The knowledge I have of my rival gives me a little cause to fear your constancy.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: My constancy! I vow –

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Do not vow –Our love is frail as is our life, and full as little in our power; and are you sure you shall outlive this day?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I am not; but when we are in perfect health 'twere an idle thing to fright ourselves with the thoughts of sudden death.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Pray what has passed between you and your father i' the garden?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: He's firm in his resolution, tell me I must marry Mrs. Harriet, or swears he'll marry himself and disinherit me; when I saw I could not prevail with him to be more indulgent, I dissembled an obedience to his will which has composed his passion, and will give us time, and I hope opportunity, to deceive him.

div2.stage: Enter OLD BELLAIR with a note in his hand.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Peace, here he comes.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Harry, take this, and let your man carry it for me to Mr. Fourbes's chamber, my lawyer, i' the Temple. [Exit YOUNG BELLAIR. [To EMILIA.] Neighbour, adod, I am glad to see thee here; make much of her, sister, she's one of the best of your acquaintance; I like her countenance and her behaviour well, she has a modesty that is not common i' this age, adod, she has.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: I know her value, brother, and esteem her accordingly.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Advise her to wear a little more mirth in her face, adod, she's too serious.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: The fault is very excusable in a young woman.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Nay, adod, I like her ne'er the worse, a melancholy beauty has her charms; I love a pretty sadness in a face which varies now and then, like changeable colours, into a smile.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Methinks you speak very feelingly, brother.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: I am but five-and-fifty, sister, you know, an age not altogether insensible! [To EMILIA.] Cheer up, sweetheart, I have a secret to tell thee may chance to make thee merry; we three will make collation together anon; i' the meantime mum, I can't abide you; go, I can't abide you. Enter YOUNG BELLAIR. Harry, come, you must along with me to my Lady Woodvil's. I am going to slip the boy at a mistress.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: At a wife, sir, you would say.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: You need not look so glum, sir; a wife is no curse when she brings the blessings of a good estate with her; but an idle town flirt, with a painted face, a rotten reputation, and a crazy fortune, adod, is the devil and all; and such a one I hear you are in league with.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I cannot help detraction, sir.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out, a pise o' their breeches, there are keeping fools enough for such flaunting baggages, and they are e'en too good for 'em. [To EMILIA.] Remember night, go, you're a rogue you're a rogue; fare you well, fare you well; come, come, come along, sir.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: On my word the old man comes on apace; I'll lay my life he's smitten.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: This is nothing but the pleasantness of his humour.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: I know him better than you; let it work, it may prove lucky.

sp.speaker: Page
sp.p: Madam, Mr. Medley has sent to know whether a visit will not be troublesome this afternoon?

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: [Exit Page. Send him word his visits never are so.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: He's a very pleasant man.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: He's a very necessary man among us women; he's not scandalous i' the least, perpetually contriving to bring good company together, and always ready to stop up a gap at ombre; then he knows all the little news o' the town.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: I love to hear him talk o' the intrigues; let 'em be never so dull in themselves, he'll make 'em pleasant i' the relation.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: But he improves things so much one can take no measure of the truth from him. Mr. Dorimant swears a flea or a maggot is not made more monstrous by a magnifying glass than a story is by his telling it.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Hold, here he comes.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Mr. Medley.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Your servant, madam.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: You have made yourself a stranger of late.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: I believe you took a surfeit of ombre last time you were here.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Indeed I had my bellyful of that termagant Lady Dealer; there never was so insatiable a carder, an old gleeker never loved to sit to't like her; I have played with her now at least a dozen times till she's worn out all her fine complexion, and her tour would keep in curl no longer.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Blame her not, poor woman; she loves nothing so well as a black ace.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: The pleasure I have seen her in when she has had hope in drawing for a matadore!

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: 'Tis as pretty sport to her as persuading masks off is to you to make discoveries.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Pray, where's your friend Mr. Dorimant?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Soliciting his affairs; he's a man of great employment has more mistresses now depending than the most eminent lawyer in England has causes.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Here has been Mrs. Loveit, so uneasy and out of humour these two days.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: How strangely love and jealousy rage in that poor woman!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: She could not have picked out a devil upon earth so proper to torment her; he has made her break a dozen or two of fans already, tear half a score points in pieces, and destroy hoods and knots without number.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: We heard of a pleasant serenade he gave her t'other night.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A Danish serenade, with kettledrums and trumpets.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Oh, barbarous!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: What, you are of the number of the ladies whose ears are grown so delicate since our operas, you can be charmed with nothing but flutes douces and French hautboys.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Leave your raillery, and tell us is there any new wit come forth, songs or novels?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A very pretty piece of gallantry by an eminent author called The Diversions of Brussels ; very necessary to be read by all old ladies who are desirous to improve themselves at questions and commands, blindman's buff, and the like fashionable recreations.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Oh, ridiculous!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Then there is The Art of Affectation , written by a late beauty of quality, teaching you how to draw up your breasts, stretch up your neck, to thrust out your breech, to play with your head, to toss up your nose, to bite your lips, to turn up your eyes, to speak in a silly soft tone of a voice, and use all the foolish French words that will infallibly make your person and conversation charming, with a short apology at the latter end, in the behalf of young ladies who notoriously wash and paint, though they have naturally good complexions.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: What a deal of stuff you tell us?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Such as the town affords, madam. The Russians hearing the great respect we have for foreign dancing have lately sent over some of their best balladines, who are now practising a famous ballet, which will be suddenly danced at the Bear Garden.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Pray forbear your idle stories, and give us an account of the state of love as it now stands.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Truly there has been some revolutions in those affairs, great chopping and changing among the old, and some new lovers, whom malice, indiscretion, and misfortune have luckily brought into play.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: What think you of walking into the next room, and sitting down before you engage in this business?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I wait upon you, and I hope (though women are commonly unreasonable) by the plenty of scandal I shall discover to give you very good content, ladies.

div2.head: SCENE II
div2.stage: Enter Mrs. LOVEIT and PERT. Mrs. LOVEIT putting up a letter, then pulling out her pocket-glass, and looking in it.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Pert.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I hate myself. I look so ill to-day.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Hate the wicked cause on't, that base man Mr. Dorimant, who makes you torment and vex yourself continually.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: He is to blame, indeed.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: To blame to be two days without sending, writing, or coming near you, contrary to his oath and covenant! 'twas to much purpose to make him swear: I'll lay my life there's not an article but he has broken –talked to the vizards i' the pit; waited upon the ladies from the boxes to their coaches; gone behind the scenes and fawned upon those little insignificant creatures the players; 'tis impossible for a man of his inconstant temper to forbear, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I know he is a devil, but he has something of the angel yet undefaced in him, which makes him so charming and agreeable that I must love him be he never so wicked.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: I little thought, madam, to see your spirit tamed to this degree, who banished poor Mr. Lackwit but for taking up another lady's fan in your presence.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: My knowing of such odious fools contributes to the making of me love Dorimant the better.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Your knowing of Mr. Dorimant, in my mind, should rather make you hate all mankind.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: So it does, besides himself.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Pray, what excuse does he make in his letter?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: He has had business.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Business in general terms would not have been a current excuse for another; a modish man is always very busy when he is in pursuit of a new mistress.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Some fop has bribed you to rail at him; he had business, I will believe it, and will forgive him.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: You may forgive him anything, but I shall never forgive him his turning me into ridicule, as I hear he does.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I perceive you are of the number of those fools his wit has made his enemies.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: I am of the number of those he's pleased to rally, madam; and if we may believe Mr. Wagfan and Mr. Caperwell, he sometimes makes merry with yourself too among his laughing companions.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Blockheads are as malicious to witty men as ugly women are to the handsome; 'tis their interest, and they make it their business to defame 'em.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: I wish Mr. Dorimant would not make it his business to defame you.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Should he, I had rather be made infamous by him than owe my reputation to the dull discretion of those fops you talk of. Enter BELINDA. Belinda!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: My dear.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You have been unkind of late.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Do not say unkind, say unhappy!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I could chide you; where have you been these two days?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Pity me rather, my dear, where I have been so tired with two or three country gentlewomen, whose conversation has been more insufferable than a country fiddle.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Are they relations?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: No, Welsh acquaintance I made when I was last year at St. Winifred's; they have asked me a thousand questions of the modes and intrigues of the town, and I have told 'em almost as many things for news that hardly were so when their gowns were in fashion.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Provoking creatures, how could you endure 'em?

p.seg: Now to carry on my plot; nothing but love could make me capable of so much falsehood; 'tis time to begin, lest Dorimant should come before her jealousy has stung her.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Did you see Dorimant there?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I did, and imagine you were there with him and have no mind to own it.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: What should make you think so?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: A lady masked in a pretty déshabillé , whom Dorimant entertained with more respect than the gallants do a common vizard.

p.seg: Dorimant at the play entertaining a mask, of heavens!
Good.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Did he stay all the while?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Till the play was done, and then led her out, which confirms me it was you.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Traitor!

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Now you may believe he had business, and you may forgive him too.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Ungrateful, perjured man!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: You seem so much concerned, my dear, I fear I have told you unawares what I had better have concealed for your quiet.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: What manner of shape had she?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Tall and slender, her motions were very genteel; certainly she must be some person of condition.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Shame and confusion be ever in her face when she shows it!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I should blame your discretion for loving that wild man, my dear; but they say he has a way so bewitching that few can defend their hearts who know him.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I will tear him from mine, or die i' the attempt.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Be more moderate.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Would I had daggers, darts, or poisoned arrows in my breast, so I could but remove the thoughts of him from thence!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Fie, fie! your transports are too violent, my dear. This may be but an accidental gallantry, and 'tis likely ended at her coach.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Should it proceed farther, let your comfort be, the conduct Mr. Dorimant affects will quickly make you know your rival, ten to one let you see her ruined, her reputation exposed to the town; a happiness none will envy her but yourself, madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Whoe'er she be, all the harm I wish her is, may she love him as well as I do, and may he give her as much cause to hate him!

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Never doubt the latter end of your curse, madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: May all the passions that are raised by neglected love, jealousy, indignation, spite, and thirst of revenge, eternally rage in her soul as they do now in mine!

div2.stage: [Walks up and down with a distracted air.

sp.speaker: Page
sp.p: Madam, Mr. Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I will not see him.

sp.speaker: Page
sp.p: I told him you were within, madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Say you lied, say I'm busy, shut the door; say anything.

sp.speaker: Page
sp.p: He's here, madam.

sp.speaker: Dorimant

lg.l: They taste of death who do at Heaven arrive,
But we this paradise approach alive.

sp.p: [To LOVEIT.] What, dancing the galloping nag without a fiddle? [Offers to catch her by the hand; she flings away and walks on. I fear this restlessness of the body, madam. [Pursuing her.] proceeds from an unquietness of the mind. What unlucky accident puts you out of humour; a point ill washed, knots spoiled i' the making up, hair shaded awry, or some other little mistake in setting you in order?

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: A trifle, I my opinion, sir, more inconsiderable than any you mention.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Oh, Mrs. Pert, I never knew you sullen enough to be silent; come, let me know the business.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: The business, sir, is the business that has taken you up these two days; how have I seen you laugh at men of business, and now to become a man of business yourself!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: We are not masters of our own affections, our inclinations daily alter; now we love pleasure, and anon we shall dote on business: human frailty will have it so, and who can help it?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Faithless, inhuman, barbarous man! –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Good, now the alarm strikes. –

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Without sense of love, of honour, or of gratitude, tell me –for I will know– what devil, masked she was, you were with at the play yesterday?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Faith, I resolved as much as you, but the devil was obstinate and would not tell me.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: False in this as in your vows to me! you do know.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The truth is, I did all I could to know.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: And dare you own it to my face? Hell and furies!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Spare your fan, madam; you are growing hot, and will want it to cool you.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Horror and distraction seize you, sorrow and remorse gnaw your soul, and punish all your perjuries to me! –

sp.speaker: Dorimant

lg.l: So thunder breaks the cloud in twain,
And makes a passage for the rain.

sp.p: [Turning to BELINDA. Belinda, you are the devil that have raised this storm; you were at the play yesterday, and have been making discoveries to your dear.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: You're the most mistaken man i' the world.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: It must be so, and here I vow revenge; resolve to pursue and persecute you more impertinently than ever any loving fop did his mistress, hunt you i' the Park, trace you i' the Mall, dog you in every visit you make, haunt you at the plays and i' the drawing room, hang my nose in your neck, and talk to you whether you will or no, and ever look upon you with such dying eyes, till your friends grow jealous of me, send you out of town, and make the world suspect your reputation. [In a lower voice. At my Lady Townley's when we go from hence.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I'll meet you there.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Enough.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Stand off, you sha' not stare upon her so.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Good! There's one made jealous already.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Is this the constancy you vowed?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Constancy at my years! 'tis not a virtue in season; you might as well expect the fruit the autumn ripens i' the spring.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Monstrous principle!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Youth has a long journey to go, madam: should I have set up my rest at the first inn I lodged at, I should never have arrived at the happiness I now enjoy.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Dissembler, damned dissembler!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am so, I confess; good nature and good manners corrupt me. I am honest in my inclinations, and would not, were't not to avoid offence, make a lady a little in years believe I think her young, wilfully mistake art for nature, and seem as fond of a thing I am weary of as when I doted on't in earnest.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: False man!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: True woman!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Now you begin to show yourself!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Love gilds us over and makes us show fine things to one another for a time, but soon the gold wears off, and then again the native brass appears.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Think on your oaths, your vows and protestations, perjured man.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I made 'em when I was in love.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: And therefore ought they not to bind? Oh, impious!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What we swear at such a time may be a certain proof of a present passion; but to say truth, in love there is no security to be given for the future.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Horrid and ungrateful, begone, and never see me more.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am not one of those troublesome coxcombs, who because they were once well received take the privilege to plague a woman with their love ever after; I shall obey you, madam, though I do myself some violence.

div2.stage: [He offers to go, and LOVEIT pulls him back.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Come back, you sha' not go. Could you have the ill-nature to offer it?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: When love grows diseased, the best thing we can do is to put it to a violent death; I cannot endure the torture of a lingering and consumptive passion.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Can you think mine sickly?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Oh, 'tis desperately ill! What worse symptoms are there than your being always uneasy when I visit you, your picking quarrels with me on slight occasions, and in my absence kindly listening to the impertinences of every fashionable fool that talks to you?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: What fashionable fool can you lay to my charge?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Why, the every cock-fool of all those fools, Sir Fopling Flutter.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I never saw him in my life but once.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The worse woman you, at first sight to put on all your charms, to entertain him with that softness in your voice and all that wanton kindness in your eyes you so notoriously affect when you design a conquest.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: So damned a lie did never malice yet invent. Who told you this?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: No matter; that ever I should love a woman that can dote on a senseless caper, a tawdry French ribbon, and a formal cravat.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You make me mad.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: A guilty conscience may do much; go on, be the game-mistress o' the town, and enter all our young fops as fast as they come from travel.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Base and scurrilous!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: A fine mortifying reputation 'twill be for a woman of your pride, wit, and quality!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: This jealousy's a mere pretence, a cursed trick of your own devising; I know you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Believe it, and all the ill of me you can: I would not have a woman have the least good thought of me that can think well of Fopling; farewell; fall to, and much good may [it] do you with your coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Stay, oh! stay, and I will tell you all.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have been told too much already.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Call him again.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: E'en let him go, a fair riddance.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Run, I say; call him again. I will have him called.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: The devil should carry him away first, were it my concern.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: He's frightened me from the very thoughts of loving men; for heaven's sake, my dear, do not discover what I told you; I dread his tongue as much as you ought to have done his friendship.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: He's gone, madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Lightning blast him!

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: When I told him you desired him to come back, he smiled, made a mouth at me, flung into his coach, and said –

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: What did he say?

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: " Drive away "; and then repeated verses.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Would I had made a contract to be a witch, when first I entertained this greater devil, monster, barbarian; I could tear myself in pieces. Revenge, nothing but revenge can ease me: plague, war, famine, fire, all that can bring universal ruin and misery on mankind; with joy I'd perish to have you in my power but this moment

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Follow, madam; leave her not in this outrageous passion.

lg.l: He's given me the proof which I desired of his love:
But 'tis a proof of his ill-nature too;
I wish I had not seen him use her so.
I sigh to think that Dorimant may be
One day as faithless and unkind to me.

div2.head: SCENE I. –
div2.stage: Enter HARRIET and BUSY her woman.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Dear madam! Let me set that curl in order.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Let me alone, I will shake 'em all out of order.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Will you never leave this wildness?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Torment me not.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Look! there's a knot falling off.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Let it drop.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: But one pin, dear madam.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: How do I daily suffer under thy officious fingers!

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Ah, the difference that is between you and my Lady Dapper! How uneasy she is if the least thing be amiss about her!

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: She is indeed most exact; nothing is ever wanting to make her ugliness remarkable.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Jeering people say so.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Her powdering, painting, and her patching never fail in public to draw the tongues and eyes of all the men upon her.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: She is indeed a little too pretending.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: That women should set up for beauty as much in spite of nature as some men have done for wit!

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: I hope, without offence, one may endeavour to make oneself agreeable.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Not when 'tis impossible. Women then ought to be no more fond of dressing than fools should be of talking. Hoods and modesty, masks and silence, things that shadow and conceal: they should think of nothing else.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Jesu! madam, what will your mother think is become of you? For heaven's sake, go in again.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I won't.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: This is the extravagant'st thing that ever you did in your life, to leave her and a gentleman who is to be your husband.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: My husband! Hast thou so little wit to think I spoke what I meant when I overjoyed her in the country with a low curtsey and What you please, madam, I shall ever be obedient?

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Nay, I know not, you have so many fetches.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: And this was one to get her up to London; nothing else, I assure thee.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Well, the man, in my mind, is a fine man.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: The man indeed wears his clothes fashionably, and has a pretty negligent way with him, very courtly and much affected; he bows, and talks, and smiles so agreeably as he thinks.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: I never saw anything so genteel.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Varnished over with good breeding many a blockhead makes a tolerable show.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: I wonder you do not like him.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I think I might be brought to endure him, and that is all a reasonable woman should expect in a husband; but there is duty i' the case –and like the haughty Merab,

lg.l: I find much aversion in my stubborn mind,
Which is bred by being promised and design'd.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: I wish you do not design your own ruin! I partly guess your inclinations, madam, –that Mr. Dorimant –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Leave your prating, and sing some foolish song or other.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: I will; the song you love so well ever since you saw Mr. Dorimant.

lg.l: When first Amintas charm'd my heart,
My heedless sheep began to stray;
The wolves soon stole the greatest part,
And all will now be made a prey.
Ah! let not love your thoughts possess,
'Tis fatal to al shepherdess;
The dang'rous passion you must shun,
Or else, like me, be quite undone.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Shall I be paid down by a covetous parent for a purchase? I need no land; no, I'll lay myself out all in love. It is decreed –

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: What generous resolution are you making, madam?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Only to be disobedient, sir.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Let me join hands with you in that.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: With all my heart; I never thought I should have given you mine so willingly. Here I, Harriet –

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: And I, Harry –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Do solemnly protest –

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: And vow –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: That I with you –

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: And I with you –

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Will never marry.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: A match!

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: And no match! How do you like this indifference now?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: You expect I should take it ill, I see.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: 'Tis not unnatural for you women to be a little angry [if] you miss a conquest, though you would slight the poor man were he in your power.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: There are some, it may be, have an eye like Bartholomew, big enough for the whole fair, but I am not of the number, and you may keep your gingerbread: 'twill be more acceptable to the lady whose dear image it wears, sir.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I must confess, madam, you came a day after the fair.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: You own then you are in love.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: The confidence is generous, and in return I could almost find in my heart to let you know my inclinations.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Are you in love?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Yes, with this dear town, to that degree I can scarce endure the country in landscapes and in hangings.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: What a dreadful thing 'twould be to be hurried back to Hampshire?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Ah! name it not!

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: As for us, I find we shall agree well enough! Would we could do something to deceive the grave people!

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Could we delay their quick proceeding, 'twere well; a reprieve is a good step towards the getting of a pardon.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: If we give over the game we are undone; what think you of playing it on booty?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Pretend to be in love with one another; 'twill make some dilatory excuses we may feign pass the better.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Let us do't, if it be but for the dear pleasure of dissembling.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Can you play your part?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I know not what it is to love, but I have made pretty remarks by being now and then where lovers meet. Where did you leave their gravities?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I' th' next room; your mother was censuring our modern gallant.

div2.stage: Enter OLD BELLAIR and Lady WOODVIL.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Peace! Here they come, I will lean against this wall and look bashfully down upon my fan, while you like an amorous spark modishly entertain me.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Never go about to excuse 'em; come, come, it was not so when I was a young woman.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, they're something disrespectful.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Quality was then considered, and not rallied by every fleering fellow.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Youth will have its jest, adod it will.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: 'Tis good breeding now to be civil to none but players and Exchange women; they are treated by 'em as much above their condition as others are below theirs.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out, a pise on 'em! talk no more; the rogues ha got an ill habit of preferring beauty, no matter where they find it.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: See your son and my daughter, they have improved their acquaintance since they were within.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, methinks they have; let's keep back and observe.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Now for a look and gestures that may persuade 'em I am saying all the passionate things imaginable.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Your head a little more on one side, ease yourself on your left leg, and play with your right hand.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Thus, is it not?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Now set your right leg firm on the ground, adjust your belt, then look about you.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: A little exercising will make me perfect.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Smile, and turn to me again very sparkish.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Will you take your turn and be instructed?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: At one motion play your fan, roll your eyes, and then settle a kind look upon me.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: So.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Now spread your fan, look down upon it, and tell the sticks with a finger.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Very modish!

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Clap your hand up to your bosom, hold down your gown; shrug a little, draw up your breasts, and let 'em fall again gently, with a sigh or two, etc.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: By the good instructions you give, I suspect you for one of those malicious observers who watch people's eyes and from innocent looks make scandalous conclusions.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I know some, indeed, who, out of mere love to mischief, are as vigilant as jealousy itself, and will give you an account of every glance that passes at a play and i' th' circle.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: 'Twill not be amiss now to seem a little pleasant.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Clap your fan then in both your hands, snatch it to your mouth, smile, and with a lively motion fling your body a little forwards. So, –now spread it; fall back on the sudden, cover your face with it, and break out in to a loud laughter – take up! look grave, and fall a-fanning of yourself –admirably well acted.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I think I am pretty apt at these matters.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, I like this well.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: This promises something.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Come! there is love i' th' case, adod there is, or will be; what say you, young lady?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: All in good time, sir; you expect we should fall to and love, as gamecocks fight, as soon as we are set together; adod, you're unreasonable!

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, sirrah, I like thy wit well.

sp.speaker: Servant
sp.p: The coach is at the door, madam.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Go, get you and take the air together.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Will not you go with us?

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out a pise. Adod, I ha' business and cannot. We shall meet at night at my sister Townley's.

p.seg: He's going to Emilia. I overheard him talk of a collation.

div2.head: SCENE II
div2.stage: Enter Lady TOWNLEY, EMILIA, and Mr. MEDLEY.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: I pity the young lovers we last talked of; though, to say truth, their conduct has been so indiscreet they deserve to be unfortunate.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You've had an exact account, from the great lady i' th' box down to the little orange-wench.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: You're a living libel, a breathing lampoon; I wonder you are not torn in pieces.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: What think you of setting up an office of intelligence for these matters? The project may get money.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: You would have great dealings with country ladies.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: More than Muddiman has with their husbands.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Belinda, what has been become of you? we have not seen you here of late with your friend Mrs. Loveit.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Dear creature, I left her but no so sadly afflicted.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: With her old distemper, jealousy?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Dorimant has played her some new prank.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Well, that Dorimant is certainly the worst man breathing.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: I once thought so.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: And do you not think so still?

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: No, indeed!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Oh, Jesu!

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: The town does him a great deal of injury, and I will never believe what it says of a man I do not know again, for his sake.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: You make me wonder!

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: He's a very well-bred man.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: But strangely ill-natured.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Then he's a very witty man.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: But a man of no principles.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Your man of principles is a very fine thing indeed!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: To be preferred to men of parts by women who have regard to their reputation and quiet. Well, were I minded to play the fool, he should be the last man I'd think of.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: He has been the first in many lady's favours, though you are so severe, madam.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: What he may be for a lover I know not, but he's a very pleasant acquaintance, I am sure.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Had you seen him use Mrs. Loveit as I have done, you would never endure him more.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: What, he has quarrelled with her again?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Upon the slightest occasion; he's jealous of Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: She never saw him in her life but yesterday, and that was there.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: On my conscience, he's the only man in town that's her aversion; how horribly out of humour she was all the while he talked to her!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: And somebody has wickedly told him –

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Here he comes.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Dorimant! you are luckily come to justify yourself – here's a lady –

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Has a word or two to say to you from a disconsolate person.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You tender your reputation too much, I know, madam, to whisper with me before this good company.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: To serve Mrs. Loveit, I'll make a bold venture.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Here's Medley, the very spirit of scandal.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: No matter!

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: 'Tis something you are unwilling to hear, Mr. Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Tell him, Belinda, whether he will or no.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: [aloud] Mrs. Loveit –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Softly, these are laughers, you do not know 'em.

p.seg: In a word, you've made me hate you, which I thought you never could have done.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: In obeying your commands.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: 'Twas a cruel part you played! how could you act it?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Nothing is cruel to a man who could kill himself to please you; remember, five o'clock to-morrow morning.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I tremble when you name it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Be sure you come.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I sha' not.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Swear you will.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I dare not.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Swear, I say.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: By my life! by all the happiness I hope for –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You will.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Kind.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I am glad I've sworn, I vow I think I should ha' failed you else!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Surprisingly kind! In what temper did you leave Loveit?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Her raving was prettily over, and she began to be in a brave way of defying you and all your works. Where have you been since you went from thence?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I looked in at the play.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I have promised, and must return to her again.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Persuade her to walk in the Mall this evening.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: She hates the place, and will not come.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Do all you can to prevail with her.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: For what purpose?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Sir Fopling will be here anon; I'll prepare him to set upon her there before me.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: You persecute her too much; but I'll do all you'll ha' me.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [aloud] Tell her plainly, 'tis grown so dull a business I can drudge on no longer.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: There are afflictions in love, Mr. Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You women make 'em, who are commonly as unreasonable in that as you are at play; without the advantage be on your side a man can never quietly give over when he's weary.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: If you would play without being obliged to complaisance, Dorimant, you should play in public places.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Ordinaries were a very good thing for that, but gentlemen do not of late frequent 'em; the deep play is now in private houses.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Belinda, are you leaving us so soon?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I am to go to the Park with Mrs. Loveit, madam.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: This confidence will go nigh to spoil this young creature.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: 'Twill do her good, madam. Young men who are brought up under practising lawyers prove the abler counsel when they come to be called to the Bar themselves.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The town has been very favourable to you this afternoon, my Lady Townley; you use to have an embarrass of chairs and coaches at your door, an uproar of footmen in your hall, and a noise of fools above here.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Indeed my house is the general rendezvous , and, next to the playhouse, is the common refuge of all the young idle people.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Company is a very good thing, madam, but I wonder you do not love it a little more chosen.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: 'Tis good to have an universal taste; we should love wit, but for variety be able to divert ourselves with the extravagancies of those who want it.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Fools will make you laugh.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: For once or twice; but the repetition of their folly after a visit or two grows tedious and unsufferable.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: You are a little too delicate, Emilia.

sp.speaker: Page
sp.p: Sir Fopling Flutter, madam, desires to know if you are to be seen.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Here's the freshest fool in town, and one who has not cloyed you yet. Page!

sp.speaker: Page
sp.p: Madam!

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Desire him to walk up.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Do not you fall on him, Medley, and snub him. Soothe him up in his extravagance; he will show the better.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You know I have a natural indulgence for fools, and need not his caution, sir.

div2.stage: Enter SIR FOPLING FLUTTER, with his Page after him.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Page, wait without. Madam, [To LADY TOWNLEY.] I kiss your hands. I see yesterday was nothing of chance; the belles assemblées form themselves here every day. [To EMILIA.], Lady, your servant. Dorimant, let me embrace thee; without lying, I have not met with any of my acquaintance who retain so much of Paris as thou dost –the very air thou hadst when the marquis mistook thee i' th' Tuileries, and cried, Hey! Chevalier! and then begged thy pardon.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I would fain wear in fashion as long as I can, sir; 'tis a thing to be valued in men as well as baubles.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Thou art a man of wit, and understandest the town; prithee let thee and I be intimate, there is no living without making some good man the confidant of our pleasures.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Tis true! but there is no man so improper for such a business as I am.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Prithee, why hast thou so modest an opinion of thyself?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Why, first, I could never keep a secret in my life, and then there is no charm so infallibly makes me fall in love with a woman as my knowing a friend loves her. I deal honestly with you.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Thy humour's very gallant, or let me perish; I knew a French count so like thee.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Wit, I perceive, has more power over you than beauty, Sir Fopling, else you would not have let this lady stand so long neglected.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: [to EMILIA] A thousand pardons, madam; some civilities due, of course, upon the meeting a long absent friend. The éclat of so much beauty, I confess, ought to have charmed me sooner.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: The brilliant of so much good language, sir, has much more power than the little beauty I can boast.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I never saw anything prettier than this high work on your point d'Espagne . –

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: 'Tis not so rich as point de Venise . –

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Not altogether, but looks cooler, and is more proper for the season. Dorimant, is not that Medley?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The same, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Forgive me, sir; in this embarrass of civilities I could not come to have you in my arms sooner. You understand an equipage the best of any man in town, I hear.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: By my own you would not guess it.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: There are critics who do not write, sir.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Our peevish poets will scarce allow it.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Damn 'em, they'll allow no man wit who does not play the fool like themselves, and show it! Have you taken notice of the calèche I brought over?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Oh, yes! 'T has quite another air than th' English makes.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: 'Tis as easily known from an English tumbril as an Inns of Court man is from one of us.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Truly, there is a bel-air in calèches as well as men.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: But there are few so delicate to observe it.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: The world is generally very grossier here, indeed.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Here's very fine.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Extreme proper.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: A slight suit I made to appear in at my first arrival, not worthy your consideration, ladies.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The pantaloon is very well mounted.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: The tassels are new and pretty.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I never saw a coat better cut.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: It makes me show long-waisted, and, I think, slender.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That's the shape our ladies dote on.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Your breech, though, is a handful too high in my eye, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Peace, Medley; I have wished it lower a thousand times, but a pox on't, 'twill not be.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: His gloves are well fringed, large and graceful.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I was always eminent for being bien-gante .

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: He wears nothing but what are originals of the most famous hands in Paris.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: You are in the right, madam.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: The suit?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Barroy.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: The garniture?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Le Gras.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: The shoes?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Piccat.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
