sp.p: The periwig?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Chedreux.

sp.speaker: Lady Town and Emilia
sp.p: The gloves?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Orangerie: you know the smell, ladies. Dorimant, I could find in my heart for an amusement to have a gallantry with some of our English ladies.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Tis a thing no less necessary to confirm the reputation of your wit than a duel will be to satisfy the town of your courage.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Here was a woman yesterday –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Mistress Loveit.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: You have named her.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You cannot pitch on a better for your purpose.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Prithee, what is she?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: A person of quality, and one who has a rest of reputation enough to make the conquest considerable. Besides, I hear she likes you too.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Methought she seemed, though, very reserved and uneasy all the time I entertained her.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Grimace and affectation. You will see her i' th' Mall to-night.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Prithee let thee and I take the air together.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am engaged to Medley, but I'll meet you at St. James's and give you some information upon the which you may regulate your proceedings.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: All the world will be in the Park to-night: ladies, 'twere pity to keep so much beauty longer within doors and rob the Ring of all those charms that should adorn it. –Hey, page! Enter Page, and goes out again. [Exit SIR FOPLING. See that all my people be ready. Dorimant, au revoir!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A fine mettled coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Brisk and insipid.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Pert and dull.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: However you despise him, gentlemen, I'll lay my life he passes for a wit with many.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That may very well be; nature has her cheats, stums a brain, and puts sophisticate dulness often on the tasteless multitude for true wit and good-humour. Medley, come.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I must go a little way, I will meet you i' the Mall.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I'll walk through the garden thither. [To the Women.] We shall meet anon and bow.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Not to-night; we are engaged about a business the knowledge of which may make you laugh hereafter.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Your servant, ladies.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Au revoir! as Sir Fopling says.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: The old man will be here immediately.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Let's expect him i' th' garden.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Go, you are a rogue.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: I can't abide you.

div2.head: SCENE III. –
div2.stage: Enter HARRIET and YOUNG BELLAIR, she pulling him.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Come along.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: And leave your mother?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Busy will be sent with a hue and cry after us; but that's no matter.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: 'Twill look strangely in me.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: She'll believe it a freak of mine and never blame your manners.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: What reverend acquaintance is that she has met?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: A fellow-beauty of the last King's time, though by the ruins you would hardly guess it.

div2.stage: Enter DORIMANT, and crosses the stage.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: By this time your mother is in a fine taking.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: If your friend Mr. Dorimant were but here now, that she might find me talking with him.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: She does not know him, but dreads him, I hear, of all mankind.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: She concludes if he does but speak to a woman she's undone; is on her kneed every day to pray Heav'n defend me from him.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: You do not apprehend him so much as she does.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I never saw anything in him that was frightful.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: On the contrary, have you not observed something extreme delightful in his wit and person?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: He's agreeable and pleasant I must own, but he does so much affect being so, he displeases me.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Lord, madam, all he does and says is so easy and so natural.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Some men's verses seem so to the unskilful, but labour i' the one and affectation in the other to the judicious plainly appear.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I never heard him accused of affectation before.

div2.stage: Enter DORIMANT, and stares upon her.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: It passes on the easy town, who are favourably pleased in him to call it humour.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Tis she! it must be she, that lovely hair, that easy shape, those wanton eyes, and all those melting charms about her mouth which Medley spoke of; I'll follow the lottery, and put in for a prize with my friend Bellair.

lg.l: In love the victors from the vanquish'd fly:
They fly that wound, and they pursue that die.

div2.stage: Enter YOUNG BELLAIR and HARRIET, and after them DORIMANT, standing at a distance.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Most people prefer High Park to this place.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: It has the better reputation, I confess; but I abominate the dull diversions there, the formal bows, the affected smiles, the silly by-words, and amorous tweers in passing; here one meets with a little conversations now and then.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: These conversations have been fatal to some of your sex, madam.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: It may be so; because some who want temper have been undone by gaming, must others who have it wholly deny themselves the pleasure of play?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Trust me, it were unreasonable, madam.

div2.stage: [Coming up gently, and bowing to her.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Lord! who's this?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Is this the woman your father would have you marry?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Her name?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Harriet.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am not mistaken, she's handsome.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Talk to her, her wit is better than her face; we were wishing for you but now.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [to HARRIET] Overcast with seriousness o' the sudden! A thousand smiles were shining in that face but now; I never saw so quick a change of weather.

p.seg: I feel as great a change within; but he shall never know it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You were talking of play, madam; pray what may be your stint?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: A little harmless discourse in public walks, or at most a appointment in a box barefaced at the playhouse; you are for masks and private meetings where women engage for all they are worth, I hear.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have been used to deep play, but I can make one at small game when I like my gamester well.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: And be so unconcerned you'll ha' no pleasure in't.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Where there is a considerable sum to be won the hope of drawing people in makes every trifle considerable.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: The sordidness of men's natures, I know, makes 'em willing to flatter and comply with the rich, though they are sure never to be the better for 'em.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Tis in their power to do us good, and we despair not but at some time or other they may be willing.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: To men who have fared in this town like you, 'twould be a great mortification to live on hope; could you keep a Lent for a mistress?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: In expectation of a happy Easter, and though time be very precious, think forty days well lost to gain your favour.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Mr. Bellair! let us walk, 'tis time to leave him; men grow dull when they begin to be particular.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You're mistaken, flattery will not ensue, though I know you're greedy of the praises of the whole Mall.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: You do me wrong.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I do not; as I followed you I observed how you were pleased when the fops cried: "She's handsome, very handsome, By God she is," and whispered aloud your name, the thousand several forms you put your face into; then, to make yourself more agreeable, how wantonly you played with your head, flung back your locks, and looked smilingly over your shoulder at 'em.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I do not begging the men's, as you do the ladies' good liking, with a sly softness in your looks and a gentle slowness in your bows as you pass by 'em –as thus, sir; – [Acts him.] Is not this like you?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Your mother, madam.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Ah, my dear child Harriet!

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Now she is so pleased with finding her again she cannot chide her.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Come away!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Tis now but high Mall, madam the most entertaining time of all the evening.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I would fain see that Dorimant, mother, you so cry out for a monster; he's in the Mall, I hear.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Come away then! the plague is here, and you should dread the infection.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: You may be misinformed of the gentleman.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Oh, no! I hope you do not know him! He is the prince of all the devils in the town, delights in nothing but in rapes and riots.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: If you did but hear him speak, madam!

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Oh! he has a tongue, they say, would tempt the angels to a second fall.

div2.stage: Enter SIR FOPLING with his Equipage, six Footmen and a Page.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Hey, Champagne, Norman, La Rose, La Fleur, La Tour, La Verdure. Dorimant ! –

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Here, here he is among this rout, he names him ; come away, Harriet, come away.

div2.stage: [Exeunt Lady WOODVIL, HARRIET, BUSY, and YOUNG BELLAIR.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: This fool's coming has spoiled all: she's gone, but she has left a pleasing image of herself behind that wanders in my soul –It must not settle there.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: What reverie is this? Speak, man.

lg.l: Snatch'd from myself, how far behind
Already I behold the shore

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Dorimant, a discovery! I met with Bellair.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You can tell me no news, sir; I know all.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: How do you like the daughter?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You never came so near truth in your life as you did in her description.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: What think you of the mother?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Whatever I think of her, she thinks very well of me, I find.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Did she know you?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She did not; whether she does now or no, I know not. Here was a pleasant scene towards, when in came Sir Fopling, mustering up his equipage, and at the latter end named me and frighted her away.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Loveit and Belinda are not far off, I saw 'em alight at St. James's.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [whispers] Sir Fopling, hark you, a word or two. Look you do not want assurance.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I never do on these occasions.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Walk on, we must not be seen together; make your advantage of what I have told you; the next turn you will meet the lady.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Hey –Follow me all.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Medley, you shall see good sport anon between Loveit and this Fopling.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I thought there was something toward by that whisper.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You know a worthy principle of hers?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Not to be so much as civil to a man who speaks to her in the presence of him she professes to love.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have encouraged Fopling to talk to her to-night.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Now you are here she will go nigh to beat him.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: In the humour she's in, her love will make her do some very extravagant thing, doubtless.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: What was Belinda's business with you at my Lady Townley's?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: To get me to meet Loveit here in order to an éclaircissement . I made some difficulty of it, and have prepared this rencontre to make good my jealousy.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Here they come!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I'll meet her and provoke her with a deal of dumb civility in passing by, then turn short and be behind her when Sir Fopling sets upon her.

lg.l: See how unregarded now
That piece of beauty passes.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: How wonderful respectfully he bowed!

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: He's always over-mannerly when he has done a mischief.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Methought indeed at the same time he had a strange despising countenance.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: The unlucky look, he thinks, becomes him.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I was afraid you would have spoke to him, my dear.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I would have died first; he shall no more find me the loving fool he has done.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: You love him still!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: I wish you did not.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I do not, and I will have you think so. What made you hale me to this odious place, Belinda?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I hate to be hulched up in a coach; walking is much better.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Would we could meet Sir Fopling now!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Lord! would you not avoid him?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I would make him all the advances that may be.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: That would confirm Dorimant's suspicion, my dear.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: He is not jealous, but I will make him so, and be revenged a way he little thinks on.

p.seg: If she should make him jealous, that may make him fond of her again: I must dissuade her from it. Lord! my dear, this will certainly make him hate you.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: 'Twill make him uneasy, though he does not care for me; I know the effects of jealousy on men of his proud temper.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: 'Tis a fantastic remedy, its operations are dangerous and uncertain.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: 'Tis the strongest cordial we can give to dying love, it often brings it back when there's no sign of life remaining. But I design not so much the reviving his, as my revenge.

div2.stage: Enter SIR FOPLING and his Equipage.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Hey! bid the coachman send home four of his horses, and bring the coach to Whitehall; I'll walk over the Park – Madam, the honour of kissing your fair hands is a happiness I missed this afternoon at my Lady Townley's.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You were very obliging, Sir Fopling, the last time I saw you there.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: The preference was due to your wit and beauty. Madam, your servant; there never was so sweet an evening.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: 'T has drawn all the rabble of the town hither.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: 'Tis pity there's not an order made that none but the beau monde should walk here.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: 'Twould add much to the beauty of the place. See what a sort of nasty fellows are coming. Enter three ill-fashioned Fellows, singing, 'Tis not for kisses alone, etc.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Fo! Their periwigs are scented with tobacco so strong –

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: It overcomes our pulvillio – Methinks I smell the coffee-house they come from.

sp.speaker: 1 Man
sp.p: Dorimant's convenient, Madam Loveit.

sp.speaker: 2 Man
sp.p: I like the oily buttock with her.

sp.speaker: 3 Man
sp.p: What spruce prig is that?

sp.speaker: 1 Man
sp.p: A caravan lately come from Paris.

sp.speaker: 2 Man
sp.p: Peace, they smoke. There's something else to be done, etc.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: They're engaged.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: She entertains him as if she liked him.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Let us go forward; seem earnest in discourse, and show ourselves. Then you shall see how she'll use him.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Yonder's Dorimant, my dear.

p.seg: I see him, he comes insulting; but I will disappoint him in his expectation.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I sat near one of 'em at a play to-day, and was almost poisoned with a pair of cordovan gloves he wears.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Oh! filthy cordovan, how I hate the smell!

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Did you observe, madam, how their cravats hung oose an inch from their neck, and what a frightful air it gave 'em?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Oh! I took particular notice of one that is always spruced up with a deal of dirty sky-coloured ribbon.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: That's one of the walking flageolets who haunt the Mall o' nights.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Oh! I remember him; he's a hollow tooth enough to spoil the sweetness of an evening.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I have seen the tallest walk the streets with a dainty pair of boxes neatly buckled on.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: And a little footboy at his heels pocket-high, with a flat cap –a dirty face.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: And a snotty nose.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Oh –odious! there's many of my own sex with that Holborn equipage trig to Gray's Inn Walks, and now and then travel hither on a Sunday.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: She takes no notice of you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Damn her! I am jealous of a counterplot!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Your liveries are the finest, Sir Fopling. –Oh, that page! that page is the prettily'st dressed –They are all Frenchmen?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: There's one damned English blockhead among 'em, you may know him by his mien.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Oh! that's he, that's he! what do you call him?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Hey! –I know not what to call him. –

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: What's your name?

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: John Trott, madam!

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Oh, unsufferable! Trott, Trott, Trott! there's nothing so barbarous as the names of our English servants. What countryman are you, sirrah?

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: Hampshire, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Then Hampshire be your name. Hey, Hampshire!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Oh, that sound! that sound becomes the mouth of a man of quality!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Dorimant, you look a little bashful on the matter.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She dissembles better than I thought she could have done.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You have tempted her with too luscious a bait: she bites at the coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She cannot fall from loving me to that?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You begin to be jealous in earnest.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Of one I do not love?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You did love her.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The fit has long been over.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: But I have known men fall into dangerous relapses when they have found a woman inclining to another.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [to himself] He guesses the secret of my heart! I am concerned, but dare not show it lest Belinda should mistrust all I have done to gain her.

p.seg: I have watched his look, and find no alteration there: did he love her, some signs of jealousy would have appeared.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I hope this happy evening, madam, has reconciled you to the scandalous Mall; we shall have you now hankering here again.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Sir Fopling, will you walk?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I am all obedience, madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Come along then, and let's agree to be malicious on all the ill-fashioned things we meet.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: We'll make a critique on the whole Mall, madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Belinda, you shall engage –

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: To the reserve of our friends, my dear.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: No, no exceptions –

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: We'll sacrifice all to our diversion.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: All –all –

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: All.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: All? Then let it be.

div2.stage: [Exeunt Sir FOPLING, LOVEIT, BELINDA, and PERT, laughing.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Would you had brought some more of your friends, Dorimant, to have been witnesses of Sir Fopling's disgrace and your triumph.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Twere unreasonable to desire you not to laugh at me; but pray do not expose me to the town this day or two.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: By that time you hope to have regained your credit?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I know she hates Fopling, and only makes use of him in hope to work me on again; had it not been for some powerful considerations which will be removed to-morrow morning, I had made her pluck off this mask and show the passion that lies panting under.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Here comes a man from Bellair, with news of your last adventure.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am glad he sent him. I long to know the consequence of our parting.

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: Sir, my master desires you to come to my Lady Townley's presently, and bring Mr. Medley with you. My Lady Woodvil and her daughter are there.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Then all's well, Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: They have sent for the fiddles and mean to dance! He bid me tell you, sir, the old lady does not know you, and would have you own yourself to be Mr. Courtage. They are all prepared to receive you by that name.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That foppish admirer of quality who flatters the very meat at honourable tables, and never offers love to a woman below a lady-grandmother.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You know the character you are to act, I see.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: This is Harriet's contrivance –wild, witty, lovesome, beautiful and young –come along, Medley.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: This new woman would well supply the loss of Loveit.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That business must not end so; before to-morrow's sun is set I will revenge and clear it:

lg.l: And you and Loveit to her cost shall fins,
I fathom all the depths of womankind.

div1.head: ACT IV
div1.stage: The scene opens with the fiddles playing a country dance.
Enter DORIMANT, Lady WOODVIL, YOUNG BELLAIR, and Mrs. HARRIET, OLD BELLAIR, and EMILIA, Mr. MEDLEY and Lady TOWNLEY, as having just ended the dance.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: So, so, so, a smart bout, a very smart bout, adod!

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: How do you like Emilia's dancing, brother?

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Not at all, not at all.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: You speak not what you think, I am sure.

p.seg: Adod, I love her.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [to LADY WOODVIL] All people mingle nowadays, madam, and in public places women of quality have the least respect showed 'em.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I protest you say the truth, Mr. Courtage.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Forms and ceremonies, the only things that uphold quality and greatness, are now shamefully laid aside and neglected.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Well! this is not the women's age, let 'em think what they will; lewdness is the business now, love was the business in my time.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The women indeed are little beholding to the young men of this age; they're generally only dull admirers of themselves, and make their court to nothing but their periwigs and their cravats, and would be more concerned for the disordering of 'em, though on a good occasion, than a young maid would be for the tumbling of her head or handkercher.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I protest you hit 'em.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: They are very assiduous to show themselves at Court well dressed to the women of quality, but their business is with the stale mistresses of the town, who are prepared to receive their lazy addresses by industrious old lovers who have cast 'em off and made 'em easy.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: He fits my mother's humour so well, a little more and she'll dance a kissing dance with him anon.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Dutifully observed, madam.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: They pretend to be great critics in beauty; by their talk you would think they liked no face, and yet can dote on an ill one if it belong to a laundress or a tailor' daughter; they cry a woman's past her prime at twenty, decayed at four-and-twenty, old and unsufferable at thirty.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Unsufferable at thirty! That they are in the wrong, Mr. Courtage, at five-and-thirty there are living proofs enough to convince 'em.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Ay, madam, there's Mrs. Setlooks, Mrs. Droplip, and my Lady Loud; show me among all our opening buds a face that promises so much beauty as the remains of theirs.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: The depraved appetite of this vicious age tastes nothing but green fruit, and loathes it when 'tis kindly ripened.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Else so many deserving women, madam, would not be so untimely neglected.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I protest, Mr. Courtage, a dozen such good men as you would be enough to atone for that wicked Dorimant and all the under-debauchees of the town. [HARRIET, EMILIA, YOUNG BELLAIR, MEDLEY, and Lady TOWNLEY break out into a laughter. What's the matter there?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A pleasant mistake, madam, that a lady has made, occasions a little laughter.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Come, come, you keep 'em idle, they are impatient till the fiddles play again.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You are not weary, madam?

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: One dance more; I cannot refuse you, Mr. Courtage.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: You are very active, sir.

div1.stage: [After the dance OLD BELLAIR singing and dancing up to EMILIA.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, sirrah, when I was a young fellow I could ha' capered up to my woman's gorget.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You are willing to rest yourself, madam?

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: We'll walk into my chamber and sit down.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Leave us Mr. Courtage, he's a dancer, and the young ladies are not weary yet.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: We'll send him out again.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: If you do not quickly, I know where to send for Mr. Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: This girl's head, Mr. Courtage, is ever running on that wild fellow.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Tis well you have got her a good husband, madam; that will settle it.

div1.stage: [Exeunt Lady TOWNLEY, Lady WOODVIL, and DORIMANT.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: [to EMILIA] Adod, sweetheart, be advised, and do not throw thyself away on a young idle fellow.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: I have no such intention, sir.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Have a little patience, thou shalt have the man I spake of. Adod, he loves thee, and will make a good husband; but no words.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: But, sir. –

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: No answer –out a pise! peace! and think on't.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Your company is desired within, sir.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: I go, I go, good Mr. Courtage – [To EMILIA.] Fare you well; go, I'll see you no more.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: What have I done, sir?

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: You are ugly, you are ugly; is she not, Mr. Courtage?

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Better words, or I shan't abide you.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out a pise –adod, what does she say? Hit her a pat for me there.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You have charms for the whole family.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You'll spoil all with some unseasonable jest, Medley.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You see I confine my tongue and am content to be a bare spectator, much contrary to my nature.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Methinks, Mr. Dorimant, my Lady Woodvil is a little fond of you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Would her daughter were!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: It may be you may find her so; try her, you have an opportunity.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: And I will not lose it. Bellair, here's a lady has something to say to you.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I wait upon her. Mr. Medley, we have both business with you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Get you all together then. [To HARRIET.] That demure curtsey is not amiss in jest, but do not think in earnest it becomes you.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Affectation is catching, I find; from your grave bow I got it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Where had you all that scorn and coldness in your look?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: From nature, sir; pardon my want of art: I have not learnt those softness and languishing which now in faces are so much in fashion.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You need 'em not; you have a sweetness of your own, if you would but calm your frowns and let it settle.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: My eyes are wild and wandering like my passions, and cannot yet be tied to rules of charming.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Women, indeed, have commonly a method of managing those messengers of love; now they will look as if they would kill, and anon they will look as if they were dying. They point and rebate their glances the better to invite us.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I like this variety well enough, but hate the set face that always looks as it would say, Come, love me –a woman who at plays makes the doux yeux to a whole audience and at home cannot forbear 'em to her monkey.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Put on a gentle smile, and let me see how well it will become you.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I am sorry my face does not please you as it is, but I shall not be complaisant and change it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Though you are obstinate, I know 'tis capable of improvement, and shall do you justice, madam, if I chance to be at Court when the critics of the circle pass their judgment; for thither you must come.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: And expect to be taken in pieces, have all my features examined, every motion censured, and on the whole be condemned to be put pretty, or a beauty of the lowest rate. What think you?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The women, nay, the very lovers who belong to the drawing-room, will maliciously allow you more than that; they always grant what is apparent that they may the better be believed when they name concealed faults they cannot easily be disproved in.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Beauty runs as great a risk exposed at Court as wit does on the stage, where the ugly and the foolish all are free to censure.

p.seg: I love her, and dare not let her know it; I fear she has an ascendant o'er me, and may revenge the wrongs I have done her sex.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: You make me start! I did not think to have heard of love from you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I never knew what 'twas to have a settled ague yet, but now and then have had irregular fits.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Take heed! sickness after long health is commonly more violent and dangerous.

p.seg: I have took the infection from her, and feel the disease now spreading in me –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: 'Twill do little execution out of your mouth on me, I am sure.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: It has been fatal –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: To some easy women, but we are not all born to one destiny; I was informed you use to laugh at love and not make it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The time has been, but now I must speak –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: If it be on that idle subject, I will put on my serious look, turn my head carelessly from you, drop my lip, let my eyelids fall and hang half o'er my eyes –thus– while you buzz a speech of an hour long in my ear, and I answer never a word; why do you not begin?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That the company may take notice how passionately I make advances of love, and how disdainfully you receive 'em.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: When your love's grown strong enough to make you bear being laughed at, I'll give you leave to trouble me with it: till when, pray forbear, sir.

div1.stage: Enter Sir FOPLING and others in masks.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What's here, masquerades?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I thought that foppery had been left off and people might have been in private with a fiddle.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Tis endeavoured to be kept on foot still by some who find themselves the more acceptable the less they are known.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: This must be Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: That extraordinary habit shows it.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: What are the rest?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A company of French rascals whom he picked up in Paris and has brought over to be his dancing equipage on these occasions. Make him own himself; a fool is very troublesome when he presumes he is incognito.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: [to HARRIET] Do you know me?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Ten to one but I guess at you.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Are you women as fond of a vizard as we men are?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I am very fond of a vizard that covers a face I do not like, sir.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Here are no masks, you see, sir, but those which came with you; this was intended a private meeting, but because you look like a gentleman, if you will discover yourself, and we know you to be such, you shall be welcome.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: [pulling off his mask] Dear Bellair.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Sir Fopling! how came you hither?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Faith, as I was coming late from Whitehall, after the King's couchée , one of my people told me he had heard fiddles at my Lady Townley's, and –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You need not say any more, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Dorimant, let me kiss thee.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [whispers] Hark you, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Enough, enough –Courtage. A pretty kind of young woman that, Medley; I observed her in the Mall; more éveillée than our English women commonly are; prithee, what is she?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: The most noted coquette in town; beware of her.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Let her be what she will, I know how to take my measures; in Paris the mode is to flatter the prude , laugh at the faux-prude , make serious love to the demi-prude , and only rally with the coquette . Medley, what think you?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: That for all this smattering of the mathematics, you may be out in your judgment at tennis.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: What a coq-à-l'âne is this? I talk of women, and thou answer'st tennis.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Mistakes will be for want of apprehension.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I am very glad of the acquaintance I have with this family.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: My lady truly is a good woman.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Ah! Dorimant –Courtage I would say –would thou hadst spent the last winter in Paris with me. When thou wert there La Corneus and Sallyes were the only habitudes we had; a comedian would have been a bonne fortune . No stranger ever passed his time so well as I did some months before I came over. I was well received in a dozen families where all the women of quality used to visit; I have intrigues to tell thee more pleasant than ever thou read'st in a novel.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Write 'em, sir, and oblige us women; our language wants such little stories.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Writing, madam, 's a mechanic part of wit; a gentleman should never go beyond a song or a billet.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Bussy was a gentleman.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Who, d'Ambois?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Was there ever such a brisk blockhead?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Not d'Ambois, sir, but Rabutin –he who writ The Loves of France .

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: That may be madam: many gentlemen do things that are below 'em. Damn your authors, Courtage; women are the prettiest things we can fool away our time with.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I hope ye have wearied yourself to-nigh at Court sir, and will not think of fooling with anybody here.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I cannot complain of my fortune there, madam – Dorimant –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Again!

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Courtage, a pox on't! I have something to tell thee. When I had made my court within, I came out and flung myself upon the mat under the state i' th' outward room i' th' midst of half a dozen beauties who were withdrawn to jeer among themselves, as they called it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Did you know 'em?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Not one of 'em by heavens! not I. But they were all your friends.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: How are you sure of that?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Why we laughed at all the town; spared nobody but yourself; they found me a man for their purpose.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I know you are malicious to your power.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: And faith I had occasion to show it for I never saw more gaping fools at a ball or on a Birthday.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You learned who the women were?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: No matter; they frequent the drawing-room.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: And entertain themselves pleasantly at the expense of all the fops who come there.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: That's their business; faith, I sifted 'em, and find they have a sort of wit among them –Ah! filthy.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Look, he has been pinching the tallow candle.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: How can you breathe in a room where there's grease frying? Dorimant, thou art intimate with my lady, advise her for her own sake, and the good company that comes hither, to burn wax lights.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: What are these masquerades who stand so obsequiously at a distance?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: A set of balladins whom I picked out of the best in France, and brought over with a flutes douces or two, my servants; they shall entertain you.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I had rather see you dance yourself, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: And I had rather do it –all the company knows it –but, madam –

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Come, come, no excuses, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: By heavens, Medley!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Like a woman, I find you must be struggled with before one brings you to what you desire.

p.seg: Can he dance?

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: And fence and sing too, if you'll believe him.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: He has no more excellence in his heels than in his head. He went to Paris a plain bashful English blockhead, and is returned a fine undertaking French fop.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I cannot prevail.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Do not think it want of complaisance, madam.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: You are too well bred to want that, Sir Fopling. I believe it want of power.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: By heavens! and so it is. I have sat up so damned late and drunk so cursed hard since I came to this lewd town, that I am fit for nothing but low dancing now, a corant, bourée , or a menuet ; but St. André tells me, if I will but be regular, in one month I shall rise again. Pox on this debauchery!

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: I have heard your dancing much commended.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: It had the good fortune to please in Paris. I was judged to rise within an inch as high as the basque , in an entry I danced there.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I am mightily taken with this fool; let us sit. Here's a seat, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: At your feet, madam; I can be nowhere so much at ease: by your leave, gown.

sp.speaker: Harriet and Emilia
sp.p: Ah! you'll spoil it.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: No matter, my clothes are my creatures; I make 'em to make my court to you ladies. Hey, – [TROTT dances. qu'on commence! To an English dancer English motions. I was forced to entertain this fellow, one of my set miscarrying – Oh, horrid! leave your damned manner of dancing, and put on the French air; have you not a pattern before you –pretty well! Imitation in time may bring him to something.

div1.stage: After the dance enter OLD BELLAIR, Lady WOODVIL, and Lady TOWNLEY.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Hey, adod! what have we here, a mumming?

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Where's my daughter –Harriet?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Here, here, madam. I know not but under these disguises there may be dangerous sparks; I gave the young lady warning.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Lord! I am so obliged to you, Mr. Courtage.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Lord! how you admire this man.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: What have you to except against him?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: He's a fop.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: He's not a Dorimant, a wild extravagant fellow of the times.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: He's a man made up of forms and commonplaces sucked out of the remaining lees of the last age.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: He's so good a man, that were you not engaged –

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: You'll have but little night to sleep in.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Lord! 'tis perfect day –

p.seg: The hour is almost come I appointed Belinda, and I am not so foppishly in love here to forget: I am flesh and blood yet.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: I am very sensible, madam.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Lord, madam!

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Look, in what a struggle is my poor mother yonder?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: She has much ado to bring out the compliment.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She strains hard for it.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: See, see! her head tottering, her eyes staring, and her under lip trembling.

p.seg: Now, now she's in the very convulsions of her civility. 'Sdeath, I shall lose Belinda. I must fright her hence; she'll be an hour in this fit of good manners else.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I have seen that face. Oh, Heav'n! 'tis the same we met in the Mall; how came he here?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: A fiddle in this town is a kind of fop-call; no sooner it strikes up but the house is besieged with an army of masquerades straight.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Lord! I tremble, Mr. Courtage; for certain Dorimant is in the company.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I cannot confidently say he is not; you had best begone. I will wait upon you; your daughter is in the hands of Mr. Bellair.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I'll see her before me. Harriet, come away.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Lights! lights!

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Light down there.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, it needs not –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Call my Lady Woodvil's coach to the door quickly.

div1.stage: [Exeunt DORIMANT and YOUNG BELLAIR, with the Ladies.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Stay, Mr. Medley, let the young fellows do that duty; we will drink a glass of wine together. 'Tis good after dancing; what mumming spark is that?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: He is not to be comprehended in few words.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Hey! La Tour.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Whither away, Sir Fopling?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I have business with Courtage –

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: He'll but put the ladies into their coach, and come up again.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: In the meantime I'll call for a bottle.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Where's Dorimant?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Stolen home; he has had business waiting for him there all this night, I believe, by an impatience I observed in him.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Very likely; 'tis but dissembling drunkenness, railing at his friends, and the kind soul will embrace the blessing and forget the tedious expectation.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I must speak with him before I sleep.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Emilia and I are resolved on that business.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Peace, here's your father.

div1.stage: Enter OLD BELLAIR and Butler, with a bottle of wine.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: The women are all gone to bed. Fill, boy; Mr. Medley, begin a health.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: [whispers] To Emilia.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out, a pise! she's a rogue, and I'll not pledge you.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I know you will.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, drink it then.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Let us have the new bachique .

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, that is a hard word; what does it mean, sir'

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: A catch or drinking song.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Let us have it then.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Fill the glasses round, and draw up in a body. Hey! music!

lg.l: (They sing) The pleasures of love and the joys of good wine
To perfect our happiness wisely we join.
We to beauty all day
Give the sovereign sway,
And her favourite nymphs devoutly obey.
At the plays we are constantly making our court,
And when they are ended we follow the sport,
To the Mall and the Park,
Where we love till 'tis dark;
Then sparkling champagne
Puts an end to their reign;
It quickly recovers
Poor languishing lovers,
Makes us frolic and gay, and drowns all our sorrow;
But, alas! we relapse again on the morrow.
Let ev'ry man stand
With his glass in his hand,
And briskly discharge at the word of command.
Here's a health to all those
Whom to-night we depose:
Wine and beauty by turns great souls should inspire.
Present altogether, and now, boys, give fire!

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, a pretty business, and very merry.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Hark you, Medley, let you and I take the fiddles, and go waken Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: We shall do him a courtesy, if it be as I guess. For after the fatigue of this night, he'll quickly have his bellyful, and be glad of an occasion to cry: Take away, Handy.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I'll go with you, and there we'll consult about affairs, Medley.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: [looks at his watch] Adod, 'tis six o'clock.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Let's away then.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Mr. Medley, my sister tells me you are an honest man, and, adod, I love you. Few words and hearty –that's the way with old Harry, old Harry.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Light your flambeaux . Hey!

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: What does the man mean?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: 'Tis day, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: No matter. Our serenade will look the greater.

div2.head: SCENE II. –
div2.stage: DORIMANT'S Lodging. A table, a candle, a toilett, etc.
Enter DORIMANT in his gown, and BELINDA.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Why will you be gone so soon?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Why did you stay out so late?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Call a chair, Handy. [Exit HANDY. What makes you tremble so?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I have a thousand fears about me. Have I not been seen, think you?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: By nobody but myself and trusty Handy.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Where are all your people?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have dispersed 'em on sleeveless errands. What does that sigh mean?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Can you be so unkind to ask me? –Well– [Sighs.] were it to do again –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: We should do it, should we not?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I think we should; the wickeder man you to make me love so well. Will you be discreet now?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: You cannot.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Never doubt it.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I will not expect it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You do me wrong.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: You have no more power to keep the secret than I had not to trust you with it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: By all the joys I have had, and those you keep in store –

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: You'll do for my sake what you never did before –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: By that truth thou hast spoken, a wife shall sooner betray herself to her husband –

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Yet I had rather you should be false in this, than in another thing you promised me.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: That you would never see Loveit more but in public places, in the Park, at Court, and plays.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Tis not likely a man should be fond of seeing a damned old play when there is a new one acted.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I dare not trust your promise.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You may.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: This does not satisfy me. You shall swear you never will see her more.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I will! A thousand oaths –By all–

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Hold –You shall not, now I think on't better.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I will swear.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I shall grow jealous of the oath, and think I owe your truth to that, not to your love.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Then, by my love, no other oath I'll swear.

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: Here's a chair.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Let me go.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I cannot.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Too willingly, I fear.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Too unkindly feared. When will you promise me again?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Not this fortnight.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You will be better than your word.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I think I shall. Will it not make you love me less? [Starting.] Hark! what fiddles are these?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Look out Handy.

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: Mr. Medley, Mr. Bellair, and Sir Fopling; they are coming up.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: How got they in?

sp.speaker: Handy
sp.p: The door was open for the chair.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Lord! let me fly –

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Here, here, down the back stairs. I'll see you into your chair.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: No, no, stay and receive 'em, and be sure you keep your word and never see Loveit more: let it be a proof of your kindness.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: It shall –Handy, direct, her. Everlasting love go along with thee.

div2.stage: Enter YOUNG BELLAIR, MEDLEY, and Sir FOPLING.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Not a-bed yet!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You have had an irregular fit, Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: And is it off already?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Nature has done her part, gentlemen; when she falls kindly to work, great cures are effected in little time, you know.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: We thought there was a wench in the case by the chair that waited. Prithee make us a confidence .

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Excuse me.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Le sage Dorimant! was she pretty ?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: So pretty she may come to keep her coach and pay parish duties if the good humour of the age continue.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: And be of the number of the ladies kept by public-spirited men for the good of the whole town.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Well said, Medley.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: See, Sir Fopling dancing.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You are practising and have a mind to recover, I see.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Prithee, Dorimant, why hast not thou a glass hung up there? A room is the dullest thing without one.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Here is company to entertain you.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: But I mean in case of being alone. In a glass a man may entertain himself.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The shadow of himself indeed.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Correct the errors of his motions and his dress.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I find, Sir Fopling, in your solitude you remember the saying of the wise man, and study yourself.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: 'Tis the best diversion in our retirements. Dorimant, thou art a pretty fellow, and wear'st thy clothes well, but I never saw thee have a handsome cravat. Were they made up like mine, they'd give another air to thy face. Prithee let me send my man to dress thee but one day. By heavens! an Englishman cannot tie a ribbon.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: They are something clumsy-fisted.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I have brought over the prettiest fellow that ever spread a toilet; he served some time under Merille, the greatest genie in the world for a valet-de-chambre .

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What, he who formerly belonged to the Duke of Candale?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: The same, and got him his immortal reputation.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You've a very fine brandenburgh on, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: It serves to wrap me up after the fatigue of a ball.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I see you often in it, with your periwig tied up.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: We should not always be in a set dress; 'tis more en cavalier to appear now and then in a déshabillé .

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Pray how goes your business with Loveit?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: You might have answered yourself in the Mall last night. Dorimant! did you not see the advances she made me? I have been endeavouring at a song.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Already!

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: 'Tis my coup d'essai in English; I would fain have thy opinion of it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Let's see it.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Hey, page! give me my song –Bellair, here, thou hast a pretty voice, sing it.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Sing it yourself, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Excuse me.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: You learnt to sing in Paris.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I did, of Lambert, the greatest master in the world; but I have his own fault, a weak voice, and care not to sing out of a ruelle .

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: A ruelle is a pretty cage for a singing fop, indeed.

lg.l: (reads the song) How charming Phyllis is! how fair!
Ah, that she were as willing
To ease my wounded heart of care,
And make her eyes less killing!
I sigh! I sigh! I languish now,
And love will not let me rest;
I drive about the Park, and bow
Still as I meet my dearest.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Sing it, sing it, man; it goes to a pretty new tune, which I am confident was made by Baptiste.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Sing it yourself, Sir Fopling; he does not know the tune.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: I'll venture.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Ay, marry, now 'tis something. I shall not flatter you, Sir Fopling; there is not much thought in't, but 'tis passionate, and well turned.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: After the French way.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: That I aimed at. Does it not give you a lively image of the thing? Slap down goes the glass, and thus we are at it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: It does indeed. I perceive, Sir Fopling, you'll be the very head of the sparks who are lucky in compositions of this nature.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: La Tour, is the bath ready?

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Adieu donc, mes chers .

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: When have you your revenge on Loveit, Dorimant ?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I will but change my linen, and about it.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: The powerful considerations which hindered have been removed then?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Most luckily this morning; you must along with me, my reputation lies at stake there.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I am engaged to Bellair.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What's your business?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Ma-tri-mony, an't like you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: It does not, sir.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: It may in time, Dorimant; what think you of Mrs. Harriet?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What does she think of me?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: I am confident she loves you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: How does it appear?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Why, she's never well but when she's talking of you; but then she finds all the faults in you she can. She laughs at all who commend you; but then she speaks ill of all who do not.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Women of her temper betray themselves by their over-cunning. I had once a growing love with a lady who would always quarrel with me when I came to see her, and yet was never quiet if I stayed a day from her.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: My father is in love with Emilia.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That is a good warrant for your proceedings: go on and prosper; I must to Loveit. Medley, I am sorry you cannot be a witness.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Make her meet Sir Fopling again in the same place, and use him ill before me.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That may be brought about, I think. I'll be at your aunt's anon, and give you joy, Mr. Bellair.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: You had not best think of Mrs. Harriet too much; without church security there's no taking up there.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I may fall into the snare too. But

lg.l: The wise will find a difference in our fate;
You wed a woman, I a good estate.

div2.head: SCENE III
div2.stage: Enter the Chair with BELINDA; the Men set it down and open it. BELINDA starting.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: [surprised] Lord! where am I? in the Mall? Whither have you brought me?

sp.speaker: 1 Chairman
sp.p: You gave us no directions, madam.

p.seg: The fright I was in made me forget it.

sp.speaker: 1 Chairman
sp.p: We use to carry a lady from the squire's hither.

p.seg: This is Loveit; I am undone if she sees me. Quickly carry me away.

sp.speaker: 1 Chairman
sp.p: Whither, an't like your honour?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Ask no questions.

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: Have you seen my lady, madam?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I am just come to wait upon her.

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: She will be glad to see you, madam. She sent me to you this morning to desire your company, and I was told you went out by five o'clock.

p.seg: More and more unlucky!

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: Will you walk in, madam?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I'll discharge my chair and follow. Tell your mistress I am here. [Exeunt Footman. [Gives the Chairmen money. Take this, and if ever you should be examined, be sure you say you took me up in the Strand, over against the Exchange, as you will answer it to Mr. Dorimant.

sp.speaker: Chairmen
sp.p: We will, an't like your honour.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Now to come off, I must on –

lg.l: In confidence and lies some hope is left;
'Twere hard to be found out in the first theft.

div2.head: SCENE I
div2.stage: Enter Mistress LOVEIT and PERT, her woman.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Well, in my eyes Sir Fopling is no such despicable person.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You are an excellent judge!

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: He's as handsome a man as Mr. Dorimant, and as great a gallant.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Intolerable! is't not enough I submit to his impertinences, but I must be plagued with yours too?

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Indeed, madam –

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: 'Tis false, mercenary malice –

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: Mrs. Belinda, madam –

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: What of her?

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: She's below.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: How came she?

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: In a chair; ambling Harry brought her.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: He bring her! His chair stands near Dorimant's door, and always brings me from thence –Run and ask him where he took her up; go, there is no truth in friendship neither. Women as well as men –all are false, or all are so to me at least.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: You are jealous of her too.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You had best tell her I am. 'Twill become the liberty you take of late. This fellow's bringing of her, her going out by five o'clock –I know not what to think. Enter BELINDA. Belinda, you are grown an early riser, I hear.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Do you not wonder, my dear, what made me abroad so soon?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You do not use to be so.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: The country gentlewomen I told you of (Lord! they have the oddest diversions!) would never let me rest till I promised to go with them to the markets this morning to eat fruit and buy nosegays.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Are they so fond of a filthy nosegay?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: They complain of the stinks of the town, and are never well but when they have their noses in one.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: These are essences and sweet waters.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Oh! they cry out upon perfumes they are unwholesome; one of 'em was falling into a fit with the smell of these narolii .

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Methinks, in complaisance you should have had a nosegay too.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Do you think, my dear, I could be so loathsome to trick myself up with carnations and stock gillyflowers? I begged their pardon, and told them I never wore anything but orange flowers and tuberose. That which made me willing to go was a strange desire I had to eat some fresh nectarines.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: And had you any?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: The best I ever tasted.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Whence came you now?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: From their lodgings, where I crowded out of a coach, and took a chair to come and see you, my dear.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Whither did you send for that chair?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: 'Twas going by empty.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Where do these country gentlewomen lodge, I pray?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: In the Strand, over against the Exchange.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: That place is never without a nest of 'em; they are always as one goes by fleering in balconies or staring out of windows.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: [whispers to the Footman] Come hither.

p.seg: This fellow by her order has been questioning the chairmen –I threatened 'em with the name of Dorimant; if they should have told truth I am lost for ever.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: In the Strand, said you?

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: Yes, madam, over against the Exchange.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: She's innocent, and I am much to blame.

p.seg: I am so frighted my countenance will betray me.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Belinda! what makes you look so pale?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Want of my usual rest, and jolting up and down so long in an odious hackney.

sp.speaker: Footman
sp.p: Madam, Mr. Dorimant!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: What makes him here?

p.seg: Then I am betrayed indeed; he's broke his word, and I love a man that does not care for me.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Lord! you faint, Belinda.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I think I shall; such an oppression here on the sudden.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: She has eaten too much fruit, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Not unlikely!

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: 'Tis that lies heavy on her stomach.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Have her into chamber, give her some surfeit water, and let her lie down a little.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: Come, madam, I was a strange devourer of fruit when I was young, so ravenous –

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Oh, that my love would be put calm awhile! that I might receive this man all the scorn and indignation he deserves.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Now for a touch of Sir Fopling to being with. Hey – page –give positive order that none of my people stir –let the canaille wait as they should do: since noise and nonsense have such powerful charms,

lg.l: I, that I may successful prove,
Transform myself to what you love.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: If that would do, you need not change from what you are; you can be vain and loud enough.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: But not with so good a grace as Sir Fopling. Hey, Hampshire! –Oh! that sound! that sound becomes the mouth of a man of quality.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Is there a thing so hateful as a senseless mimic?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: He's a great grievance indeed to all who like yourself, madam, love to play the fool in quiet.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: A ridiculous animal who has more of the ape than the ape has of the man in him.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have as mean an opinion of a sheer mimic as yourself; yet were he all ape I should prefer him to the gay, the giddy, brisk, insipid, noisy fool you dote on.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Those noisy fools, however you despise 'em, have good qualities, which weigh more (or ought at least) with us women than all the pernicious wit you have to boast of.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That I may hereafter have a just value for their merit, pray do me the favour to name 'em.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You'll despise 'em as the dull effects of ignorance and vanity, yet I care not if I mention some. First, they really admire us, while you at best but flatter us well.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Take heed! fools can dissemble too –

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: They may, but not so artificially as you: there is no fear they should deceive us. Then they are assiduous, sir; they are ever offering us their service, and always waiting on our will.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You owe that to their excessive idleness; they know not how to entertain themselves at home, and find so little welcome abroad, they are fain to fly to you who countenance 'em as a refuge against the solitude they would be otherwise condemned to.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Their conversation too diverts us better.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Playing with your fan, smelling to your gloves, commending your hair, and taking notice how 'tis cut and shaded after the new way.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Were it sillier than you can make it, you must allow 'tis pleasanter to laugh at others than to be laughed at ourselves, though never so wittily. Then though they want skill to flatter us, they flatter themselves so well they save us the labour; we need not take that care and pains to satisfy 'em of our love, which we so often lose on you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: They commonly indeed believe too well of themselves, and always better of you than you deserve.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You are in the right; they have an implicit faith in us which keeps 'em from prying narrowly into our secrets, and saves us the vexations trouble of clearing doubts which your subtle and causeless jealousies every moment raise.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: There is an inbred falsehood in women which inclines 'em still to them whom they may most easily deceive.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: The man who loves above his quality does not suffer more from the insolent impertinence of his mistress than the woman who loves above her understanding does from the arrogant presumptions of her friend.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You mistake the use of fools: they are designed for properties, and not for friends. You have an indifferent stock of reputation left yet. Lose it all like a frank gamester on the square; 'twill then be time enough to turn rook and cheat it up again on a good substantial bubble.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: The old and the ill-favoured are only fit for properties indeed, but young and handsome fools have met with kinder fortunes.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: They have, to the shame of your sex be it spoken; 'twas this, the thought of this, made me, by a timely jealousy, endeavour to prevent the good fortune you are providing for Sir Fopling – but against a woman's frailty all our care is vain.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Had I not with a dear experience bought the knowledge of your falsehood, you might have fooled me yet. This is not the first jealousy you have feigned to make a quarrel with me and get a week to throw away on some such unknown inconsiderable slut as you have been lately lurking with at plays.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Women, when they would break off with a man, never want th' address to turn the fault on him.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You take a pride of late in using of me ill, that the town may know the power you have over me, which now (as unreasonably as yourself) expects that I (do me all the injuries you can) must love you still.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am so far from expecting that you should, I begin to think you never did love me.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Would the memory of it were so wholly worn out in me that I did doubt it too! What made you come to disturb my growing quiet?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: To give you joy of your growing infamy.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Insupportable! insulting devil! this from you, the only author of my shame! This from another had been but justice, but from you 'tis a hellish and inhuman outrage. What have I done?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: A thing that puts you below my scorn and makes my anger as ridiculous as you have made my love.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I walked last night with Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You did, madam, and you talked and laughed aloud, ha, ha, ha! –Oh! that laugh! that laugh becomes the confidence of a woman of quality.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You, who have more pleasure in the ruin of a woman's reputation than in the endearments of her love, reproach me not with yourself, and I defy you to name the man can lay a blemish on my fame.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: To be seen publicly so transported with the vain follies of that notorious fop, to me is an infamy below the sin of prostitution with another man.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Rail on, I am satisfied in the justice of what I did; you had provoked me to't.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What I did was the effect of a passion whose extravagances you have been willing to forgive.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: And what I did was the effect of a passion you may forgive if you think fit.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Are you so indifferent grown?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I am.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Nay! then 'tis time to part. I'll send you back your letters you have so often asked for. I have two or three of 'em about me.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Give 'em me.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You snatch as if you thought I would not –there– and may the perjuries in 'em be mine if e'er I see you more.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Stay!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I will not.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You shall.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What have you to say?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I cannot speak it yet.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Something more in commendation of the fool. Death! I want patience, let me go.

p.seg: I cannot. I can sooner part with the limbs that hold him. I hate that nauseous fool, you know I do.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Was it the scandal you were fond of then?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You'd raised my anger equal to my love, a thing you ne'er could do before, and in revenge I did –I know not what I did. –Would you would not think on't any more!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Should I be willing to forget it, I shall be daily minded of it, 'twill be a commonplace for all the town to laugh at me; and Medley, when he is rhetorically drunk, will ever be declaiming on it in my ears.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: 'Twill be believed a jealous spite! Come, forget, it.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Let me consult my reputation; you are too careless of it. [pauses.] You shall meet Sir Fopling in the Mall again to-night.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: What mean you?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have thought on it, and you must: 'tis necessary to justify my love to the world; you can handle a coxcomb as he deserves when you are not out of humour, madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Public satisfaction for the wrong I have done you! This is some new device to make me more ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Hear me.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I will not.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You will be persuaded.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Are you so obstinate?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Are you so base?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You will not satisfy my love?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I would die to satisfy that, but I will not to save from a thousand racks do a shameless thing to please your vanity.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Farewell, false woman!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Do! go!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You will call me back again.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Exquisite fiend! I knew you came but to torment me.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [surprised] Belinda here!

p.seg: He starts and looks pale; the sight of me has touched his guilty soul.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: 'Twas but a qualm, as I said, a little indigestion; the surfeit water did it, madam, mixed with a little mirabilis .

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I am confounded, and cannot guess how she came hither!

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: 'Tis your fortune, Belinda, ever to be here when I am abused by this prodigy of ill-nature.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I am amazed to find him here! How has he the face to come near you?

p.seg: Here is fine work towards! I never was at such a loss before.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: One who makes a public profession of breach of faith and ingratitude; I loathe the sight of him.

p.seg: There is no remedy; I must submit to their tongues now, and some other time bring myself off as well as I can.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Other men are wicked, but then they have some sense of shame: he is never well but when he triumphs, nay, glories to a woman's face in his villainies.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You are in the right, Belinda; but methinks your kindness for me makes you concern yourself too much with him.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: It does indeed, my dear; his barbarous carriage to you yesterday made me hope you ne'er would see him more, and the very next day to find him here again provokes me strangely; but, because I know you love him, I have done.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You have reproached me handsomely, and I deserve it for coming hither; but –

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: You must expect it, sir; all women will hate you for my lady's sake.

p.seg: Nay, if she begins too, 'tis time to fly; I shall be scolded to death else. I am to blame in some circumstances, I confess; but as to the main, I am not so guilty as you imagine. I shall seek a more convenient time to clear myself.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Do it now! what impediments are here?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I want time, and you want temper.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: These are weak pretences!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You were never more mistaken in your life, and so farewell.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Call a footman, Pert, quickly; I will have him dogged.

sp.speaker: Pert
sp.p: I wish you would not for my quiet and your own.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I'll find out the infamous cause of all our quarrels, pluck her mask off, and expose her barefaced to the world.

p.seg: Let me but escape this time I'll never venture more.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Belinda! you shall go with me.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I have such a heaviness hangs on me with what I did this morning, I would fain go home and sleep, my dear.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Death and eternal darkness! I shall never sleep again. Raging fevers seize the world, and make mankind as restless all as I am!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: I knew him false, and helped to make him so. Was not her ruin enough to fright me from the danger? It should have been, but love can take no warning.

div2.head: SCENE II. –
div2.stage: Enter MEDLEY, YOUNG BELLAIR, Lady TOWNLEY, EMILIA, and Chaplain.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Bear up, Bellair, and do not let us see that repentance in thine we daily do in married faces.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: This wedding will strangely surprise my brother when he knows it.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Your nephew ought to conceal it for a time, madam, since marriage has lost its good name; prudent men seldom expose their own reputations till 'tis convenient to justify their wives.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: [without] Where are you all there? Out, adod, will nobody hear?

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: My brother! quickly, Mr. Smirk, into this closet; you must not be seen yet.

div2.stage: Enter OLD BELLAIR and Lady TOWNLEY's Page.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Desire Mr. Fourbes to walk into the lover parlour, I will be with him presently. [To YOUNG BELLAIR.] Where have you been, sir, you could not wait on me to-day?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: About a business.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Are you so good at business? Adod, I have a business too you shall despatch out of hand, sir. Send for a parson, sister; my Lady Woodvil and her daughter are coming.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: What need you huddle up things thus?

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out a pise! youth is apt to play the fool, and 'tis not good it should be in their power.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: You need not fear your son.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: He's been idling this morning, and, adod, I do not like him. [To EMILIA] How dost thou do, sweetheart?

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: You are very severe, sir; married in such haste.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Go to, thou'rt a rogue, and I will talk with thee anon. Here's my Lady Woodvil come. Enter Lady WOODVIL, HARRIET, and BUSY. Welcome, madam; Mr. Fourbes is below with the writings.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Let us down, and make an end then.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Sister, show the way. [To YOUNG BELLAIR, who is talking to HARRIET.] Harry, your business lies not there yet; excuse him till we have done, lady, and then, adod, he shall be for thee. Mr. Medley, we must trouble you to be a witness.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: I luckily came for that purpose, sir.

div2.stage: [Exeunt OLD BELLAIR, MEDLEY, YOUNG BELLAIR, Lady TOWNLEY, and Lady WOODVIL.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: What will you do, madam?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Be carried back and mewed up in the country again, run away here, anything rather than be married to a man I do not care for –Dear Emilia, do thou advise me.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Mr. Bellair is engaged, you know.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I do; but know not what the fear of losing an estate may fright him to.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: In the desperate condition you are in you should consult with some judicious man; what think you of Mr. Dorimant?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I do not think of him at all.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: She thinks of nothing else, I am sure.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: How fond your mother was of Mr. Courtage!

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Because I contrived the mistake to make a little mirth you believe I like the man.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Mr. Bellair believes you love him.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Men are seldom in the right when they guess at a woman's mind; would she whom he loves loved him no better!

p.seg: That's e'en well enough, on all conscience.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Mr. Dorimant has a great deal of wit.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: And takes a great deal of pains to show it.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: He's extremely well-fashioned.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Affectedly grave or ridiculous wild and apish.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: You defend him still against your mother.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I would not were he justly rallied, but I cannot hear any one undeservedly railed at.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Has your woman learnt the song you were so taken with?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I was fond of a new thing; 'tis dull at second hearing.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Mr. Dorimant made it.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: She knows it, madam, and has made me sing it at least a dozen times this morning.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Thy tongue is as impertinent as thy fingers.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: You have provoked her.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: 'Tis but singing the song, and I shall appease her.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Prithee do.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: She has a voice will grate your ears worse than a cat-call, and dresses so ill she's scarce fit to trick up a yeoman's daughter on a holiday.
