lg.l: [sings.] As Amoret with Phyllis sat
One evening on the plain,
And saw the charming Strephon wait
To tell the nymph his pain,
The threat'ning danger to remove
She whisper'd in her ear,
Ah, Phyllis! if you would not love,
This shepherd do not hear.
None ever had so strange an art
His passion to convey
Into a list'ning virgin's heart,
And steal her soul away.
Fly, fly betimes, for fear you give
Occasion for your fate.
In vain, said she, in vain I strive,
Alas! 'tis now too late.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Music so softens and disarms the mind –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: That not one arrow does resistance find.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Let us make use of the lucky minute then.

p.seg: My love springs with my blood into my face, I dare not look upon him yet.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What have we here, the picture of celebrated beauty giving audience in public to a declared lover?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Play the dying fop and make the piece complete, sir.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: What think you if the hint were well improved –the whole mystery of making love pleasantly designed and wrought in a suit of hangings?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: 'Twere needless to execute fools in effigy who suffer daily in their own persons.

p.seg: Mrs. Bride, for such I know this happy day has made you.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: Defer the formal joy you are to give me and mind your business with her. [Aloud] Here are dreadful preparations, Mr. Dorimant, writings sealing, and a parson sent for.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: To marry this lady?

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Condemned she is, and what will become of her I know not, without you generously engage in a rescue.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: In this sad condition, madam, I can do no less than offer you my service.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: The obligation is not great; you are the common sanctuary for all young women who run from their relations.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have always my arms pen to receive the distressed. But I will open my heart, and receive you where none yet did ever enter: you have filled it with a secret, might I but let you know it –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Do not speak it if you would have me believe it; your tongue is so famed for falsehood 'twill do the truth an injury.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Turn not away then; but look on me and guess it.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Did you not tell me there was no credit to be given to faces? that women nowadays have their passions as much at will as they have their complexions, and put on joy and sadness, scorn and kindness, with the same ease they do their paint and patches –Are they the only counterfeits?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You wrong your own while you suspect my eyes; by all the hope I have in you, the inimitable colour in your cheeks is not more free from art than are the sighs I offer.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: In men who have been long hardened in sin we have reason to mistrust the first signs of repentance.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The prospect of such a heaven will make me persevere and give you marks that are infallible.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: What are those?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I will renounce all the joys I have in friendship and in wine, sacrifice to you all the interest I have in other women –

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Hold! –though I wish you devout I would not have you turn fanatic –Could you neglect these awhile and make a journey into the country?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: To be with you I could live there and never send one thought to London.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Whate'er you say, I know all beyond High Park's a desert to you, and that no gallantry can draw you farther.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: That has been the utmost limit of my love, but now my passion knows no bounds, and there's no measure to be taken of what I'll do for you from anything I ever did before.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: When I hear you talk thus in Hampshire I shall begin to think there may be some truth enlarged upon.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Is this all? –will you not promise me?–

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I hate to promise! What we do then is expected from us, and wants much of the welcome it finds when it surprises.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: May I not hope?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: That depends on you and not on me; and 'tis to no purpose to forbid it.

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Faith, madam, now I perceive the gentleman loves you too; e'en let him know your mind, and torment yourselves no longer.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Dost think I have no sense of modesty?

sp.speaker: Busy
sp.p: Think, if you lose this you may never have another opportunity.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: May he hate me –a curse that frights me when I speak it –if ever I do a thing against the rules of decency and honour!

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [to EMILIA] I am beholding to you for your good intentions, madam.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: I thought the concealing of our marriage from her might have done you better service.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Try her again.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: What have you resolved, madam? The time draws near.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: To be obstinate, and protest against this marriage.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: [To EMILIA] Quickly, quickly, let Mr. Smirk out of the closet.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: A parson! had you laid him in here?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I knew nothing of him.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Should it appear you did, your opinion of my easiness may cost you dear.

div2.stage: Enter OLD BELLAIR, YOUNG BELLAIR, MEDLEY, and Lady WOODVIL.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out a pise! the canonical hour is almost past. Sister, is the man of God come?

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: He waits your leisure.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: By your favour, sir. Adod, a pretty spruce fellow! what may we call him?

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Mr. Smirk, my Lady Biggot's chaplain.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: A wise woman! adod, she is. The man will serve for the flesh as well as the spirit. Please you, sir, to commission a young couple to go to bed together i' God's name? Harry.

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: Here, sir.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out a pise! without your mistress in your hand!

sp.speaker: Smirk
sp.p: Is this the gentleman?

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Smirk
sp.p: Are you not mistaken, sir?

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, I think not, sir.

sp.speaker: Smirk
sp.p: Sure you are, sir.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: You look as if you would forbid the banns; Mr. Smirk, I hope you have no pretension to the lady?

sp.speaker: Smirk
sp.p: Wish him joy, sir! I have done him the good office to-day already.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out a pise! what do I hear?

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Never storm, brother, the truth is out.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: How say you, sir? is this your wedding-day?

sp.speaker: Young Bellair
sp.p: It is, sir.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: And, adod, it shall be mine too; give me thy hand, sweetheart. [To EMILIA] What dost thou mean? give me thy hand, I say.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Come, come, give her your blessings; this is the woman your son loved and is married to.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Ha! cheated! cozened! and by your contrivance, sister!

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: What would you do with her? She's a rogue and you can't abide her.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Shall I hit her a pat for you, sir?

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, you are all rogues, and I never will forgive you.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Whither! whither away?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Let him go and cool awhile.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: [to DORIMANT] Here's a business broke out now; Mr. Courtage, I am made a fine fool of.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: You see the old gentleman knew nothing of it.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I find he did not. I shall have some trick put upon me if I stay in this wicked town any longer. Harriet! dear child! where art thou? I'll into the country straight.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, madam, you shall hear me first.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Hither my man dogged him.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Yonder he stands, my dear.

p.seg: And with him the face that has undone me! Oh, that I were but where I might throw out the anguish of my heart! here it must rage within and break it.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Mrs. Loveit, are you afraid to come forward?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I was amazed to see so much company here in a morning, the occasion sure is extraordinary.

p.seg: Loveit and Belinda! the devil owes me a shame to-day, and I think never will have done paying it.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Married! dear Emilia! how am I transported with the news?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: [to DORIMANT] I little thought Emilia was the woman Mr. Bellair was in love with; I'll chide her for not trusting me with the secret.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: How do you like Mrs. Loveit?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: She's a famed mistress of yours, I hear.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: She has been on occasion.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: [to Lady WOODVIL] Adod, madam, I cannot help it.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: You need make no more apologies, sir.

sp.speaker: Emilia
sp.p: [to LOVEIT] The old gentleman's excusing himself to my Lady Woodvil.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! I never heard of anything so pleasant.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: [to DORIMANT] She's extremely overjoyed at something.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: At nothing; she is one of those hoiting ladies who gaily fling themselves about and force a laugh when their aching hearts are full of discontent and malice.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Oh, Heav'n! I was never so near killing myself with aughing. Mr. Dorimant, are you a brideman?

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Mr. Dorimant! Is this Mr. Dorimant, madam?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: If you doubt it, your daughter can resolve you, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I am cheated too, basely cheated.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out a pise! what's here? more knavery yet?

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Harriet! on my blessing, come away, I charge you.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Dear mother, do but stay and hear me.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I am betrayed, and thou art undone, I fear.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Do not fear it. I have not, nor ever will do anything against my duty; believe me, dear mother, do.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: [to LOVEIT] I had trusted you with this secret, but that I knew the violence of your nature would ruin my fortune, as now unluckily it has. I thank you, madam.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: She's an heiress, I know, and very rich.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: To satisfy you I must give up my interest wholly to my love; had you been a reasonable woman, I might have secured 'em both and been happy.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You might have trusted me with anything of this kind, you know you might. Why did you go under a wrong name?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: The story is too long to tell you know –be satisfied, this is the business, this is the mask has kept me from you.

p.seg: He's tender of my honour, though he's cruel to my love.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Was it no idle mistress then?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Believe me, a wife, to repair the ruins of my estate that needs it.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: The knowledge of this makes my grief hang lighter on my soul; but I shall never more be happy.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Belinda!

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Do not think of clearing yourself with me, it is impossible. Do all men break their words thus?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Th' extravagant words they speak in love; 'tis as unreasonable to expect we should perform all we promise then, as do all we threaten when we are angry. When I see you next –

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Take no notice of me, and I shall not hate you.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: How came you to Mrs. Loveit?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: By a mistake the chairmen made for want of my giving them directions.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: 'Twas a pleasant one. We must meet again.

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Never?

sp.speaker: Belinda
sp.p: When we do, may I be as infamous as you are false.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Men of Mr. Dorimant's character always suffer in the general opinion of the world.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: You can make no judgment of a witty man from common fame, considering the prevailing faction, madam.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, he's in the right.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Besides, 'tis a common error among women to believe too well of them they know and too ill of them they don't.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, he observes well.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: Believe me, madam, you will find Mr. Dorimant as civil a gentleman as you thought Mr. Courtage.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: If you would but know him better –

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: You have a mind to know him better; come away! You shall never see him more.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Dear mother, stay!

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: I wo' not be consenting to your ruin.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Were my fortune in your power –

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Your person is.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: Could I be disobedient I might take it out of yours, and put it into his.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: 'Tis that you would be at; you would marry this Dorimant?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: I cannot deny it; I would, and never will marry any other man.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Is this the duty that you promised?

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: But I will never marry him against your will –

p.seg: She knows the way to melt my heart.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: [to OLD BELLAIR] Come, sir, you have not the heart any longer to refuse your blessing.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, I ha' not –Rise, and God bless you both! Make much of her, Harry, she deserves thy kindness. [To EMILIA] Adod, sirrah, I did not think it had been in thee.

div2.stage: Enter Sir FOPLING and his Page.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: 'Tis a damned windy day; hey, page? Is my periwig right?

sp.speaker: Page
sp.p: A little out of order, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Pox o' this apartment! it wants an antechamber to adjust oneself in. [To LOVEIT] Madam, I came from your house, and your servants directed me hither.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: I will give order hereafter they shall direct you better.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: The great satisfaction I had in the Mall last night has given me much disquiet since.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: 'Tis likely to give me more than I desire.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: What the devil makes her so reserved? Am I guilty of an indiscretion, madam?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: You will be of a great one if you continue your mistake, sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Something puts you out of humour.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: The most foolish inconsiderable thing that ever did.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Is it in my power?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: To hang or drown it; do one of 'em, and trouble me no more.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: So fière ? Serviteur, madame . Medley, where's Dorimant?

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Methinks the lady has not made you those advances to-day she did last night, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Prithee do not talk of her.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: She would be a bonne fortune .

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Not to me, at present.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: An intrigue now would be put a temptation to me to throw away that vigour on one which I mean shall shortly make my court to the whole sex in a ballet .

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Wisely considered, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: No one woman is worth the loss of a cut in a caper.

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Not when 'tis so universally designed.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Mr. Dorimant, every one has spoke so much in your behalf that I can no longer doubt but I was in the wrong.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: There's nothing but falsehood and impertinence in this world; all men are villains or fools. Take example from my misfortunes, Belinda; if thou wouldst be happy, give thyself wholly up to goodness.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: [To LOVEIT] Mr. Dorimant has been your God Almighty long enough; 'tis time to think of another.

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Jeered by her! I will lock myself up in my house, and never see the world again.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: A nunnery is the more fashionable place for such a retreat, and has been the fatal consequence of many a belle passion .

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Hold, heart! till I get home; should I answer 'twould make her triumph greater.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Your hand, Sir Fopling.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Shall I wait upon you, madam?

sp.speaker: Loveit
sp.p: Legion of fools, as many devils take thee!

sp.speaker: Medley
sp.p: Dorimant! I pronounce thy reputation clear and henceforward when I would know anything of woman, I will consult no other oracle.

sp.speaker: Sir Fopling
sp.p: Stark mad, by all that's handsome! Dorimant, thou hast engaged me in a pretty business.

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: I have not leisure now to talk about it.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Out a pise! what does this Man of Mode do here again!

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: He'll be an excellent entertainment within, brother, and is luckily come to raise the mirth of the company.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: Madam, I take my leave of you.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: What do you mean, madam?

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: To go this afternoon part of my way to Hartley.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Adod, you shall stay and dine first; come, we will all be good friends, and you shall give Mr. Dorimant leave to wait upon you and your daughter in the country.

sp.speaker: Lady Woodvil
sp.p: If his occasions bring him that way, I have now so good an opinion of him he shall be welcome.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: To a great rambling lone house that looks as it were not inhabited, the family's so small; there you'll find my mother, an old lame aunt, and myself, sir, perched up on chairs at a distance in a large parlour, sitting moping like three or four melancholy birds in a spacious volery. Does not this stagger your resolution?

sp.speaker: Dorimant
sp.p: Not at all, madam. The first time I saw you you left me with the pangs of love upon me, and this day my soul has quite given up her liberty.

sp.speaker: Harriet
sp.p: This is more dismal than the country, Emilia; pity me who am going to that sad place. Methinks I hear the hateful noise of rooks already –kaw, kaw, kaw. There's music in the worst cry in London, My dill and cucumbers to pickle .

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Sister, knowing of this matter, I hope you have provided us some good cheer.

sp.speaker: Lady Townley
sp.p: I have, brother, and the fiddles too.

sp.speaker: Old Bellair
sp.p: Let 'em strike up then; the young lady shall have a dance before she departs. [Dance] [After the dance] So, now we'll in and make this an arrant wedding-day.

lg.l: And if these honest gentlemen rejoice,
Adod, the boy has made a happy choice.
Most modern wits such monstrous fools have shown,
They seem'd not of heaven's making, but their own.
Those nauseous harlequins in farce may pass,
But there goes more to a substantial ass;
Something of man must be exposed to view,
That, gallants, they may more resemble you:
Sir Fopling is a fool so nicely writ,
The ladies would mistake him for a wit,
And when he sings, talks loud, and cocks, would cry,

l.emph: I vow, methinks he's pretty company!

lg.l: So brisk, so gay, so travell'd, so refined,
As he took pains to graft upon his kind.
True fops help nature's work, and go to school
To file and finish God Almighty's fool.
Yet none Sir Fopling him, or him, can call;
He's knight o' th' shire, and represents ye all.
From each he meets he culls whate'er he can,
Legion's his name, a people in a man:
His bulky folly gathers as it goes,
And, rolling o'er you, like a snowball grows.
His various modes from various fathers follow;
One taught the toss, and one the new French wallow
His sword-knot this, his cravat this design'd,
And this the yard-long snake he twirls behind.
From one the sacred periwig he gain'd,
Which wind ne'er blew, nor touch of hat profaned
Another's diving bow he did adore,
Which with a shog casts all the hair before;
Till he, with full decorum, brings it back,
And rises with a water-spaniel shake.
As for his songs (the ladies' dear delight)
Those sure he took from most of you who write.
Yet every man is safe from what he fear'd,
For no one fool is hunted from the herd.
